fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington is getting a much chillier reception on Capitol Hill than at the White House as lawmakers from both parties use the visit to denounce China's actions on the world stage.

Lawmakers have long found little downside to taking a hawkish tone on China, but the U.S.'s war with Iran has inflamed tensions as U.S. officials accuse China of propping up Iran's economy and supplying its military with components and intelligence, endangering U.S. service members in the Middle East.

In speeches, letters, press conferences and hearings, lawmakers from both parties aired criticism of Xi's visit. Their actions and events stand in stark contrast to the warm welcome that Trump gave Xi on Wednesday as he arrived in Washington for a lavish state visit.

Sen. Roger Wicker, the chair of the Senate Armed Services Committee, took to the Senate floor Tuesday night, offering a list of issues for Trump to raise with Xi, but not before suggesting that Xi shouldn't have been asked to visit Washington at all.

"Quite frankly, had the White House asked me for advice, I would have suggested the president not invite Xi Jinping to Washington for such a lavish welcome here in the United States of America based on all of the troubling issues we have with President Xi and the Chinese Communist Party," Wicker said.

Wicker seemed particularly taken aback by the honor of a state dinner. Over the salad course, Wicker said the president could ask Xi about the Chinese Navy's harassment of Filipino fishermen and sailors. Then, while the servers are "switching from chardonnay to cabernet at the fancy state dinner," perhaps the president could turn to the issue of Taiwan, he said.

He went on to say he hopes some progress will be made when the president discussed trade and artificial intelligence with Xi. But concluded with this: "During every minute of dialogue, our commander in chief should keep in mind that his guest is a brutal, unelected, and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbors and whose massive military arsenal is aimed directly at the United States of America."

Ahead of Xi's visit, the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party released a highly critical video that had been viewed more than 245,000 times on X. In the video, the committee details Xi's rise to power starting in 1974 and ends by labeling him "the biggest opponent of freedom and liberty in the world."

The House created the panel in 2023. It's held several hearings on human rights issues in China and advocates for legislation on an array of economic and military issues. For example, the committee's chairman, Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., recently introduced a bill that would prohibit the manufacture or sale of Chinese cars in the U.S.

Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and three other Republican senators used the Xi visit to press the Trump administration to move ahead with aid and arms sales to Taiwan.

In a letter, they reminded Secretary of State Marco Rubio that he had previously stated that "deterring an invasion of Taiwan must be our top priority." And they noted Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had once declared that the U.S. "will not let our allies and partners be subordinated and intimidated."

China has pressed Washington to halt the arms sales, most prominently during a summit in May between Trump and Xi in Beijing. After that meeting, the United States paused the sale of a record-breaking $14 billion package — and Trump described arms sales to Taiwan as a "very good negotiating chip" with China.

"It is difficult to imagine how the United States might credibly project influence deterrence in the Indo-Pacific," the senators wrote, "if the price of keeping up diplomatic appearances is denying our partners key deterrent capabilities."

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and three other Democratic senators held a press conference to warn against the U.S. weakening export controls for advanced semiconductor chips and equipment. They're concerned that such exports could erase the U.S.'s lead in artificial intelligence over China.

They touched on voter concerns about the safety of artificial intelligence and contrasted Democrats' call for greater regulation with the president's call to "encourage it, not rein it in."

"We must reject the false choice Trump keeps making," Schumer told reporters. "We can and must both maintain our lead on AI by restricting China's access to our technology and put up guardrails to mitigate AI's risk."

Meanwhile, on the Senate floor, Democratic senators urged Trump to confront Xi directly about the support his country is providing Iran.

"If we want to bring this war to an end, we need to cut off the outside support that allows Iran to keep fighting, and that starts with China," said Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, the ranking Democratic lawmaker on the Senate Foreign Affairs Committee.

fullText:
They offer advice, referee card games and manage players’ tantrums – we caught up with some of the volunteer profs who keep the competitive game going at this year’s world championships

Professors may be the most revered characters in the fictional world of Pokémon (apart from perhaps the Gym Leaders). In Pokémon Red and Blue, Professor Oak greets the player in a pixelated lab coat, and later provides trainers with their first battle partner; since then, each successive generation of games has introduced another professor to aid and guide trainers through their journeys. If you’ve ever played a Pokémon game, they are often the first people that you meet, apart from your in-game mom.

But you may not know that there are also real-world Pokémon professors – volunteers who help organise the game’s competitive communities around the world. Instead of lab coats, they can be seen at events wearing red Pikachu-mascot shirts labelled “staff”, paired with black trousers and shoes.

I spoke with several of these profs at the 2026 Pokémon world championships in San Francisco, California. Not only do they happily distribute their knowledge about Pokémon, but they also serve as vital staff at the tournament, working as referees and teachers, as well as event managers.

The official Pokémon website describes the Pokémon Professor Program as a “global network of passionate and knowledgable fans” who volunteer their time to help run official Pokémon events. There were roughly 300 Pokémon professors present at the 2026 Pokémon world championships, according to a representative of the Pokémon Company International. A professor’s responsibilities depend on the game they work with and their assigned role at the event. A Pokémon professor officiating a game such as Pokémon Unite might be hyper-focused on wrangling players and providing technical support, whereas a judge for a trading card game tournament might provide competitors with hands-on guidance as they navigate their first live competitive event.

Gemma Byard, a head judge in charge of making the final call on any decisions or questions that arise, became a Pokémon professor after her son started competing in the trading card game. She says that she and the other professors help ensure the integrity of the tournament, describing what goes into the day-to-day work at worlds – such as ensuring that event officials record the results of competitions correctly.

“We’ve got to make sure that all of the match slips have the correct results on them and are signed by the players to ensure, you know, that we get the right results,” Byard said. “We have to make sure that the venue is safe for everybody that’s around. We’re constantly looking out for anything that may be unsafe, or anybody that shouldn’t be in the venue. There’s a lot to think about on top of the rulings.”

Professors often juggle multiple responsibilities on the competition floor and will travel across the world to staff an event such as the world championships. When asked about how the Pokémon Company International compensates its professors, however, most people I spoke to declined to disclose details. One Pokémon professor said that the European professors are compensated with goodies, such as a special staff kit with merchandise, whereas the professors at regional tournaments in the US are paid wages; the same professor said that the Pokémon Company International helped with travel, room and board for the event. (When asked for an official statement explaining how Pokémon professors are paid, a representative from the Pokémon Company International declined to comment.)

Evelyne de Groot travelled from the Netherlands to staff this year’s championships. Like the other Pokémon professors I spoke to, de Groot worked her way up to staffing worlds after organising local competitions in her home region. Before we spoke, she was helping usher players out of the Moscone Center after the main convention hall closed for the evening. This year, she worked at a trading card game side event called Pokémon Sisterhood League, dedicated to giving women and non-binary people a chance to compete and connect.

For her, a good Pokémon professor must balance enforcing the rules with giving competitors the tools they need to enjoy the game itself. She compared the position to working in “customer service”.

“[Players] make friendships. You see them smile. You see them have a good time, but you’re part of that,” de Groot said. “If you’re not organising it properly, if you don’t give them clear instructions, then you see some failure […] You will sometimes get questions. You need to make sure you’re knowledgable regarding that. If you don’t know what you’re doing, if you don’t know how the card game works, then you can’t help them.”

De Groot’s experience as a professor has been relatively relaxed. However, some professors must serve as referees and make contentious calls throughout the competition. For Byard, that means she sometimes needs to deal with upset players. At one point during the tournament, she had to manage a player who was upset with a ruling that didn’t go his way.

“I got called over to the table, and I said to him: ‘Look, I need you just to keep your voice down and be respectful, and we’ll talk through what’s happened.’ And he was like: ‘I don’t need to talk to you. I need to talk to the head judge,’” Byard said, chuckling. “Well, buddy, you are talking to the head judge. That’s the kind of sass that we deal with a lot.”

A difficult call can lead to controversy. Earlier this year, a ruling from a different judge at another tournament made headlines when a competitive Pokémon Go player who goes by the name Firestar73 was disqualified after winning the final at the Pokémon Orlando regional championships. Many, including the competitor himself in a statement, conceded that the decision was a “good-faith mistake”.

I asked Byard about what it’s like to make tough calls at the tournament. She said that the professors are often seen as “the bad guys”. What does she wish competitors and viewers understood about the role?

“What they don’t understand is that they’re seeing a picture, but we’re getting the entire story, and we’re making the decisions based upon that story,” she said. “That can make a real difference. And we’re the ones putting ourselves out there to right a situation that’s been broken by players. We haven’t caused any distress. We’re there just to try and put it back together again.”

Interviews for this feature took place at the Pokémon world championships in San Francisco. The writer’s travel and accommodation expenses were met by the Pokémon Company.

title: Mamdani and Spain's PM build ties as the left looks to counter the far right
description:
Two of the key faces of the left in elected office, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, met at an economic event in Manhattan on Wednesday, as world leaders gather in New York for the U.N. General Assembly.
Their meeting is the latest in a slate of encounters between left-wing U.S.
fullText:
Two of the key faces of the left in elected office, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, met at an economic event in Manhattan on Wednesday, as world leaders gather in New York for the U.N. General Assembly.

Their meeting is the latest in a slate of encounters between left-wing U.S. politicians and kindred figures abroad as they seek to forge ties to counter the rise of right-wing populism.

Organizers behind these formal and informal gatherings say the efforts to bring together U.S. left-leaning Democrats in office and their ideological counterparts aim to contend with the well-organized, growing international movement of populists in step with President Donald Trump's administration, as the anti-immigrant and nationalist Alternative for Germany party gains traction, and France's Marine Le Pen and her party, National Rally, lead in polls ahead of a presidential race next year.

Wednesday's event at Gracie Mansion, Mamdani's residence, was billed as focused on "building an economy for the many." Sánchez touted the success of Spain's minimum-wage increases as "proving that another economic model is possible."

"That is why the powerful fear us. Because day after day, we show that a different path is possible, and it works," Sánchez said at the event, which also included the prime minister of Barbados, Mia Mottley, and European Council President António Costa, who is a former socialist prime minister of Portugal.

Mamdani nodded to the efforts to collaborate with like-minded leaders, telling attendees, "It is truly a privilege to be able to learn from one another, emulate each others successes and develop strategies that imitate the great progress those in this room have achieved."

Heading into the U.N. General Assembly, Mamdani over the weekend hosted left-leaning mayors from Paris, Barcelona, Rome, Amsterdam, Mexico City and elsewhere for a summit on housing, migration and climate change. And he met this week with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, a social democrat in the same general tradition as Sánchez.

In April, politicians and world leaders convened in Barcelona for the first Global Progressive Mobilization conference, which was touted by organizers as an "alternative to conservative and far-right forces."

The event included prerecorded remarks from democratic socialists Mamdani and Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont), who revitalized that tradition in U.S. politics. But it also opened up the tent to include speeches from Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz - the 2024 Democratic vice-presidential nominee who served as a moderate "Blue Dog" Democrat in Congress - and Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Connecticut), who has embraced economic populism and urged his party to connect with voters it lost in 2024.

Giacomo Filibeck, who served on the organizing committee for April's conference, told The Washington Post that the participation of the U.S. Democrats was "instrumental" in showing how the global progressive movement can work together.

"In a nutshell, we have been rediscovering our internationalism that maybe in the past years was a bit put on the side," he added.

Democrats have long sought friends abroad. As U.S. president, especially in his first term, Barack Obama courted widespread international goodwill. But he forged a special bond with Angela Merkel of Germany's Christian Democratic Union, a center-right party at least in European terms - a different segment of the Western political spectrum than the one Mamdani is courting.

Socialists and other left-wing activists also have long organized internationally. The Sanders presidential campaign built ties to equivalent movements in Europe. The New York chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America, from which Mamdani emerged, last year hosted Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the perennial French presidential candidate and founder of the hard-left party La France Insoumise.

But as energy coalesces in the left wing of the Democratic Party - with the electoral success of some candidates aligned with or backed by the DSA, Mamdani most prominent among them - the global bridge-building has taken on a new urgency.

Johan Hassel, a senior fellow and director of Global Progress Action (GPA) at the Center for American Progress, a left-leaning think tank in Washington, said Trump's reelection in 2024 was "a game changer" that helped unify global progressives.

GPA has arranged high-level meetings between U.S. officials and center-left leaders abroad. Its most recent public convening, in Toronto this past May, included appearances by Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Michigan), former U.S. transportation secretary and potential 2028 candidate Pete Buttigieg, and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.

"The left traditionally has seen more of their differences … than their similarities. I think this is changing," Hassel said. "You're starting to see a larger democratic bloc of center-left liberals, Greens. The left that understands that something … larger is at stake."

Such politicians and movements within the U.S. and abroad, he said, "are inspiring each other" as a result of their alliances. Among the examples, he cited Mamdani's embrace of social investment in child care and housing, akin to policies long adopted by European social democrats.

Conversely, European left-wing party members made the pilgrimage to New York to canvass for Mamdani in the final weeks of his campaign. Members of Germany's anti-capitalist party Die Linke (the Left) traveled to New York to learn more about Mamdani's effort and met with his advisers.

Die Linke, whose platform is focused on lowering the cost of living and using state interventions to address the German capital's housing shortage, went on to secure a historic win in the Berlin state election Sunday.

fullText:
UNITED NATIONS (AP) — The heads of major artificial intelligence firms pleaded with the United Nations on Wednesday to set controls over the burgeoning technology they are designing in order to save the world — or, at least, its people.

"If managed poorly, I even believe AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole," said Dario Amodei, the chief executive officer of Anthropic.

"We could lose control of the future to AI," said his competitor, Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI.

Both said the countries of the world, though the U.N. Security Council, where they testified Wednesday afternoon, have to set safeguards, which would be actual controls to prevent the technology from getting too powerful to rein in. They also called for the world to make sure that the power of AI isn't concentrated in one company or country.

For world leaders, one key question about AI is this: Who should control life-and-death decisions — human or machine?

The United Nations Security Council on Wednesday huddled with top technology leaders to figure out if the increasing abilities and pervasiveness of artificial intelligence should be controlled and, if so, by who. Other lingering questions: How could it be done? When might it be just too late?

The day before, U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned of "killer robots." Experts and European leaders said that's not hyperbole but something that's already a reality or at least perilously close.

title: GB sniff Road Worlds chance with Pogacar absent
description: British riders stand a strong chance of glory at cycling's Road World Championships this weekend, with young talent beginning to blossom at elite level.
fullText:
Great Britain's impressive rider line-up for cycling's Road World Championships means the team have rarely stood a better chance of glory.

For the men, there is also the helpful factor of Slovenian superstar Tadej Pogacar being absent, after he suffered crash injuries during the Vuelta a Espana in August.

But at the same time a new generation of British cycling talent is rising, and GB riders could take the coveted winner's rainbow jersey in the men's and women's road races in Montreal this weekend.

While Pogacar crashed out of the Vuelta, the race showcased the continued emergence of 21-year-old British rider Matthew Brennan, who won five stages of the three-week endurance test for Visma Lease a Bike - a record for a Grand Tour debutant.

There are currently 49 British riders competing across the men's and women's world tours - more than ever before - and some of those will compete in this World Championship weekend.

The road race itself is much like a stage of the Tour de France, but in which riders compete in national squads, looking to out-think and out-muscle each other.

A lot of the British potential is thanks to the inspiration of British cycling's golden period, which featured great success from the likes of Team Sky, Mark Cavendish and Lizzie Deignan across the past 15 years.

Deignan won the road race in 2015, while Cavendish triumphed in 2011.

In total, British riders have won the elite road races seven times, including Tom Simpson (1965), Beryl Burton (1960 & 1967), Mandy Jones (1982) and Nicole Cooke (2008).

Amid an unpredictable performance landscape for the women, Britain's best young female riders have a chance to infiltrate the once-dominant Dutch contingent.

Tour de France Femmes winner Demi Vollering remains the sport's best overall, but Briton Zoe Backstedt's brilliant second place in Sunday's Worlds time trial was her first shot at the elite level.

She will be involved in Saturday's women's road race, and Olympic mountain bike gold medallist and Tour de France stage winner Tom Pidcock will race for the men on Sunday.

"You need a lot of faith in your team to be present at the front," Backstedt told BBC Sport. "You need to talk, hear, see and feel each other to know they are there, especially as there's no team radio.

"Obviously it's about knowing the big names to follow. If Demi or Kasia [Niewiadoma] go off the front, you know it's a dangerous move and you need to be there.

"But we've got a super strong team, and if any one of us was with them, we all could stand have a chance."

The women's road race is 180.4km long, which includes eight laps of Montreal, and the men's 273.2km race incorporates 12 circuits.

More Then the Score: How cyclists escape to victory

One key way to win a road race at the Road Worlds is by breaking away from the peloton with a certain distance of the race left to run.

The risk is that one, or a handful, of cyclists find it much harder to win a race by riding into the wind than a peloton of more than 100 riders all taking turns in what can be known as the 'washing machine effect'.

But, if the legs are good and the wind is with them, riders can break away for glory.

"Sometimes you are surprised when you hit the wall, but other times you can push harder and dig deeper," Norway's Sigrid Haugset told the BBC's More Than the Score podcast.

The Uno-X Mobility rider won stage three of this year's Tour de France Femmes after a huge 113km breakaway in which she beat more decorated rivals, such as Belgium's Lotte Kopecky.

"That's the good day - when you feel unstoppable. But I like it when there is plenty of noise [on the team radio from the car]. If it's too little, you get into your head, you feel a bit alone."

Steve Cummings is sporting director at World Tour team Jayco Alula and a former GB rider and breakaway stage winner on both the 2015 and 2016 Tours de France.

Assessing the thrill of a breakaway win, he told More Than the Score: "It's like an underdog victory, and it kind of warms the heart. You have to go all-in. It becomes unpredictable and things can happen tactically and physically - say if a rider pushes too much on a climb.

"That day [in 2015] I did the climb of my life. I was empty for two days after [the 2016 win] and I was in bed for two days after [a Dauphine stage win]. It takes a lot out of you."

title: The footballer who had a heart transplant - then became a World Cup winner
description: Martyn Jackson never thought he'd play football again when he had a heart transplant in 2024. Less than two years later, he was a World Cup winner with England.
fullText:
When Martyn Jackson walked off the pitch after Ramsbottom United's 2-1 win over Cheadle Town in October 2024, it never crossed his mind that one day he could be a World Cup winner.

In fact, in the days after that match, his goal was just staying alive.

Just a couple of days after the final whistle, Jackson started to feel unwell during the night.

He went into hospital and was diagnosed with myocarditis, an inflammation of the heart usually caused by an infection. Within weeks, he was placed on the super urgent waiting list for a transplant.

His life was saved when a donor heart became available, and on 28 November 2024, he had successful surgery at Wythenshawe Hospital in Greater Manchester.

Fast forward to September 2026, and Jackson scored for England in their 5-1 win over Spain in the final of the Transplant Football World Cup.

His team-mates and opponents were, like him, all recipients of a donor organ.

"Obviously, when you've had a transplant, you don't think you're ever going to play again. That's what I thought anyway," Jackson tells BBC Sport.

"I'll be forever grateful to my donor and the family for what they've given me. They've given me the gift of life and the opportunity to live my life to the fullest."

Football at the Transplant World Cup is not quite the same as the game played at the Fifa World Cup.

Instead, it reflects how delicate each player's body is having been through life-altering surgery.

Matches are seven-a-side and played over 20-minute halves. Contact is "not as aggressive as I was used to", Jackson says.

Having played 11-a-side football in the ninth tier of English football before his surgery, he became a game-changing new addition to the national transplant team when he joined up with the squad in January 2026.

Jackson spent his youth career in the academy at Manchester United, before spells at Blackburn Rovers, Preston North End and Burnley. He eventually stopped pursuing a career as a professional and spent 13 years with clubs across the non-league pyramid.

During his recovery, wife Lucy heard about the opportunity to join an England Transplant FC team on social media.

Daley Cross, manager of the England team, said of Lucy's role: "She was just trying to do her best for him and trying to find a way to motivate him.

"His wife did drop in the conversation that he used to play at Manchester United as a schoolboy. So that got our ears twitched instantly.

"You could tell from him being on the pitch, even though he was so fresh into his journey, that he knew the football game and he would be such an incredible asset to us.

"You can be in a dark place, at the time of diagnosis, through your treatment or even post-transplant. So to have us exist to help and inspire people means that we are getting some incredible footballers.

"And that really is the power of it: to that transplant community or to the world, showing people that when you've had organ failure, your life isn't over. There is a chance for you, and you can go and resume and live your life."

As the recipient of a donor heart, Jackson has to manage his exercise workload more carefully than his team-mates, many of whom have had kidney transplants, the most common transplant in the UK.

His role in the side tends to involve 10-minute bursts, rather than playing for the duration of matches.

Bayern Munich's Alphonso Davies was diagnosed with a mild form of myocarditis in 2022. He was sidelined for nearly five months, undergoing specialist cardiac monitoring, before returning to play.

Jackson started to feel ill two days after Ramsbottom side's win over Cheadle, and his case became so severe that doctors had to fit his heart with a mechanical pump to keep him alive.

"Of course it was extremely scary," he says, "but at that stage, when you are critically ill, there's not really much you can do about it. You have to accept it."

The super urgent waiting list he was placed on is the highest priority of the three tiers of patients waiting for a new heart. Typically, only about four or five people are on the list at any one time in the UK.

Dr Paul Callan, a consultant cardiologist at Wythenshawe Hospital's Heart and Lung Centre, worked with Jackson during his diagnosis and recovery.

"Initially, we used to quote an average wait of seven days on the urgent transplant list," he says. "Now it's up to 14 days. Maybe 10% of patients who are put on the list get too poorly and have to be taken off the list."

That increased waiting time is the result of a reduction in the numbers of organ donors in the UK, with a 9% drop recorded in 2026 compared to the same period last year. There are 8,700 people currently waiting for a donor organ, a figure that NHS Blood and Transplant say is an all-time high.

This Organ Donation Week,, external which runs from 21-28 September, the NHS has launched an urgent response plan to address the decline.

Jackson has yet to meet the family of the donor from which he received his new heart. He says he is considering reaching out to them around the two-year anniversary of his surgery.

For him to make a recovery within that time frame, culminating in playing football in a Transplant World Cup, is "remarkable", according to Dr Callan.

England beat six teams on their way to winning last Friday's final in Frankfurt, scoring 36 goals, but for every player at the tournament there is gratitude that they even have the opportunity to play a football match again.

"It is so important to spread that message, have that conversation about organ donation," says England manager Cross, "because our team only exists for that reason.

"I wouldn't have 16 players to manage if we didn't have organ donation. And England wouldn't have just gone and won a World Cup."

title: Ronaldo spurred on by 1,000 goals and Portugal glory
description: Cristiano Ronaldo contemplated retirement after the World Cup but wants to reach 1,000 career goals and help a new-look Portugal thrive before hanging up his boots.
fullText:
Cristiano Ronaldo considered retiring after the World Cup but says he opted to extend his glittering career as he believes he can help Portugal to further success - and reach a personal milestone of 1,000 career goals.

The 41-year-old confirmed in the summer that the 2026 World Cup would be his last, although his long-term future remained uncertain.

However, he has been included in Jorge Jesus' 25-man squad for Portugal's Nations League campaign, which begins against Wales in Lisbon on Thursday night.

In the lead-up to the contest with Craig Bellamy's side, the Al-Nassr forward also targeted the 21 goals needed to reach that magical 1,000 mark.

Asked if he thought about retiring from international duty after the World Cup, Ronaldo responded: "Yes, I did.

"Of course, I'm always thinking on my decisions, my future, the present also. I'm a thinker, you have to think."

The former Sporting, Manchester United, Real Madrid and Juventus player said: "I had a conversation with our president, with our coach. I still believe that I'm able to help the national team to reach what they want.

"I think I can give to the national team my support, not only through the goals, but also outside of football."

Ronaldo is a two-time Nations League winner with Portugal, and he said adding a third title was also an aim alongside his personal ambitions.

"Both aims are important," he said.

"One thousand goals, yes, and the national team. Winning the Nations League, the competition starts tomorrow [Thursday], it's a new age."

title: Zohran Mamdani Hosts the World
description: Prajwal...
fullText:
In a meeting with mayors from around the globe, Mamdani argued that the left must fix everyday problems—or the right will find someone to scapegoat for them.

On the afternoon of September 19, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani stood in front of a wastewater treatment plant at Hunts Point in the Bronx and told a group of visiting international mayors that it offered one of the best views in New York City. This was an illustration of Mamdani’s focus on the day-to-day mechanics of city government—sewage, buses, and potholes—and an argument he has been making throughout this year that the socialist left’s credibility will be rebuilt by proving that government can still make people’s lives easier.

Standing with him were the mayors of Helsinki, Barcelona, and Rome, who were part of the group of mayors and city leaders in New York over the weekend for the Urban 20, or U20, a summit of cities from G20 nations. On the sidelines of the summit, Mamdani hosted several left-wing mayors, taking them on a bus tour of New York City and showing them public housing in Brownsville. Mamdani’s office said his meetings with the mayors focused on finding solutions to housing, climate, and migration issues.

Throughout the weekend, it became clear that Mamdani’s pitch for a government that makes life easier for residents has resonated with his international counterparts. At the U20 summit on September 20, Mamdani argued that the left should reclaim phrases like “quality of life,” “efficiency,” and “waste” from the right. “If you are staring at an example of social disorder or social inefficiency, and the left refuses to explain either why it has happened or how they will fix it, then the right gets to point at someone in the immediate area and say, ‘That’s who did it,’” Mamdani said.

The same day, Mamdani said that the movement that made him mayor of New York extends far beyond the city and aims to address the crises of our times—the affordability crisis and the mass migration of millions of people due to climate change and instability. “Those fleeing war, genocide, flood, famine and instability should not be turned away but should be welcomed.… Each of us holds a shared responsibility to provide all our people with opportunity and to view migration not as an obstacle to a city’s success, but, frankly, as fundamental to that success,” Mamdani said.

Earlier this summer, the FIFA World Cup gave the soccer-fan mayor a chance to showcase his idea of a multicultural city in the face of threats from Washington. Even as FIFA priced ordinary fans out of the games, Mamdani pushed FIFA for cheaper tickets and opened up the city for pickup soccer games through the night. On game days in the New York area, Mamdani uploaded direct-to-camera videos in which he spoke about figures like Sócrates, a Brazilian legend whose club, Corinthians, opposed Brazil’s military dictatorship in the 1980s. In another video, he mentioned Brian Clough, the legendary English manager whose Derby County team stood on the picket lines during the 1972 miners’ strike.

The same political instincts were on display again this week as world leaders descended on New York. Mamdani met with Rome Mayor Roberto Gualtieri to discuss housing policy and with Mexico City Mayor Clara Brugada to hand out flyers to delivery workers informing them of their rights under local labor laws. He exchanged soccer jerseys with Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who is in a tight reelection fight against Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. And on September 22, Mamdani visited a public school with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre to discuss AI’s growing presence in classrooms. It is an area of interest for both leaders as New York followed Norway in restricting generative AI for younger students.

Mamdani’s convening of world leaders coincided with the surprise Berlin election win for Elif Eralp, the daughter of Turkish immigrants, who led Germany’s Left Party, Die Linke, to its strongest-ever result in the city on a platform focusing squarely on cost of living and housing. Outlets have already run headlines crediting the influence of Mamdani’s campaign in Berlin after a delegation of Die Linke met with Mamdani’s advisers in New York recently. It has also emerged that political organizations in Europe have studied the canvassing operation that propelled the New York mayor to his election win.

These exchanges have placed Mamdani at the center of the international left as it tries to fight the economic order that has worsened mass migration and made cities inhospitable. “At a time of division and retreat, our cities are choosing cooperation,” Mamdani said ahead of the U20 event. In his closing remarks on September 20, he added, “Familiarity allows us to communicate effectively and openly. It facilitates the lending of policy, the sharing of lessons learned, the exchange of ideas. A transit win in one city informs a newfound ambition in another. A public health success here becomes a blueprint there. That is what familiarity can do. That is the practice of solidarity in action.”

Between the reemergence of right-wing red-baiting and Donald Trump’s use of the chilling National Security Presidential Memorandum–7 to criminalize left political organizing, we’re seeing McCarthyism reborn before our eyes. 

This assault on democracy cannot be ignored or wished away. Resisting it requires bravery in the face of threats and repression, a steadfast commitment to the truth, and the unwavering belief that we can—and will—overcome this darkness.

We must have an independent media that sets the record straight, unearths corruption and abuses of power, and advances a politics of justice and dignity for all if we’re to win this fight.

That’s why I’m writing to you today. This September, The Nation needs to add 100 monthly donors to sustain our progressive journalism. Your contribution makes the next investigative report, the next truth-speaking column, and the next pathbreaking essay all possible. 

I hope you’ll support our work with a recurring donation today. If you donate $10 or more a month, we’ll send you a brand new “Hands Off the Free Press!” sticker to recognise your commitment to our cause. Please, donate today.

Onward,

fullText:
Heading into the international break, Ipswich Town have double the amount of points at this stage of the season compared with their previous Premier League campaign.

However, I can't help but feel slightly disappointed. While I probably would have taken a tally of six from the opening five matches when the fixtures were announced in June, Town's efforts have, in my opinion, warranted more.

Bear in mind as well that they've played four teams who are featuring in Europe this season.

Saturday at Hill Dickinson Stadium - against a team with just their domestic fixtures to worry about - was particularly frustrating, as Gary O'Neil's side didn't deserve to come away with nothing.

The fact that they did - and will also be without Abdul Fatawu next time because of a daft suspension - leaves a bit of a sour taste.

Let's focus on some of the positives from that afternoon on Merseyside though, beginning in goal, where Christian Walton justified the manager's big call in making a change between the posts.

I was perhaps among the minority in thinking that four games in might be too soon to drop Kjell Scherpen, but Walton looked assured and composed, just as he did when he took a similar chance last season.

He appears to have solved Town's goalkeeping conundrum with little fuss, and deserves to now be given an extended chance in the top-flight. Oh, and there was very little he could have done about Everton's somewhat freak winning goal.

Player of the match Abdoul Ouattara is another that deserves more than a mention.

The 20-year-old, making his first Premier League start, was outstanding at right-back, and justified another big call from the manager in choosing the Ivorian over the more experienced Darnell Furlong, who was so impressive during last season's run to promotion.

Town's plethora of summer arrivals have, in general, given supporters real hope that their latest Premier League stay will be an extended one.

Issa Diop has complemented Jacob Greaves or Dara O'Shea very well at centre-back, while Exequiel Palacios and Sasa Lukic are undoubtedly an upgrade on the midfield starters of two years ago .

That said, they have a long way to go before achieving the club legendary status of Sam Morsy and Massimo Luongo.

In Julio Encisio, Town have a player who can turn a game in an instant, but the surprise package for me has been Emersonn in the number nine role.

I hadn't been expecting a huge amount from the Brazil striker during the early stages of his first spell in English football but, to his credit, he has already become a fixture in the side.

The former Toulouse player has a couple of goals to his name already, and his hold-up play has been very impressive.

With that in mind, it is no surprise that Zian Flemming is still waiting for a first league start in his new club colours, but the Dutchman will be needed further down the line.

He has shown from his cameos so far that he will be ready to take any chance that comes his way.

In summary, O'Neil and his players have given themselves a very good platform from which to kick on, and Town supporters will be relishing the return of domestic football after the internationals, rather than fearing it.

fullText:
BENGALURU, India (AP) — This year's powerful El Nino and the record global heat it's driving, along with severe droughts, wildfires and shrinking water supplies, could lead to nearly half a million more deaths worldwide by the end of February, according to a research report released Wednesday.

The grim warning by the University of Chicago-based Climate Impact Lab says that as many as 451,000 more heat-related deaths between June and the end of February could be attributed to El Nino, compared with heat deaths expected in a typical year.

The heaviest toll, the group says, is expected in poorer countries, already struggling with food insecurity and high energy costs, partly due to climate change and the fallout of the war in Iran.

Michael Greenstone, a co-founder of the group and the study's co-author, said the heat danger will likely persist beyond February — even though this El Nino is expected to end by then. The fallout of the weather phenomenon could be felt well into next summer, he added.

The research, he said, shows that heat is most dangerous in places that are already hot and relatively poor.

"If you're already in a hot place, the extra couple of degrees are going to be much more dangerous," he said. Wealthier places, he added, generally have greater access to air conditioning, reliable water supplies and functioning health systems.

The study combined seasonal temperature forecasts with localized estimates of how high temperatures affect mortality across more than 24,000 regions worldwide.

Researchers estimated the additional heat-related deaths by comparing deaths expected under El Nino-driven high temperatures with deaths expected if temperatures remained similar to what they have been in the last three decades. The projected fatalities are for the entire El Nino period, from June 2026 until the end of February 2027.

The study by Greenstone and his colleagues also warns that the Global South — a term that isn't geographical but a reference to developing countries in general — will bear the heaviest burden of the excessive heat.

The researchers behind the report found that the Sahel region in Africa — countries along the semiarid southern fringe of the Sahara Desert — is expected to be the hardest-hit, with about 66,800 additional deaths caused by El Nino-driven heat.

Other major hot spots include South and Southeast Asia and parts of Latin America, according to the report. The researchers project about 19,400 additional heat-related deaths across the Philippines, Vietnam, Thailand and Cambodia, as well as 19,300 in Indonesia, 15,800 in India and 13,300 in Brazil.

With such staggering numbers, there are recommended measures that governments can take, the report says. They include heat-warning systems, cooling centers, hydration stations, protections for outdoor workers, expanded hospital capacity and targeted outreach to elderly people and other vulnerable groups.

The authors also call for what they describe as anticipatory financing, so governments can move resources before dangerous heat peaks.

Abhiyant Tiwari, a heat expert at NRDC India who was not involved in the study, said the report's projections should serve as a call to action rather than be another reason for alarm.

But while it's one thing to have well thought-out plans — as India does — implementing these plans and raising needed funds remains a challenge, he said.

"The real measure of our preparedness is not how many heat warnings we issue, but how effectively we protect people and reduce preventable deaths," Tiwari added.

El Nino is a natural climate pattern, but this year's unusually strong event is occurring on a planet already warmed by human-caused climate change, increasing the risks from extreme heat.

The Climate Impact Lab said global land temperatures during this El Nino could be higher by about 1.2 Celsius (2.1 Fahrenheit), producing 44% more extremely hot days than in a typical year. The report said those temperature increases may mirror conditions that climate change could make common some 20 years from now.

That's why this El Nino could offer a preview of what's ahead as the planet continues to warm, the report said. It's also an opportunity for decision-makers "to see exactly where emergency actions can be taken now to save tens of thousands of lives," the authors say.

The GOP backlash, which has been simmering below the surface throughout Trump's second term as lawmakers privately grumbled he hasn't focused enough on affordability issues, burst into public view as a rapid succession of Republicans challenged Trump on everything from the Iran war to the president's "lavish" summit this week with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Republicans have long been loathe to openly criticize the president, who has wielded an uncommonly strong hold over his party and retains long memories about who has crossed him. Back in May, eight Indiana state lawmakers who defied Trump on a redistricting plan faced their primary voters, and only two won. The president that month similarly ended Texas Senator John Cornyn's political career by backing Ken Paxton's primary challenge instead.

So confident is the president of his singular electoral magnetism that his rallying cry at campaign events from Texas to North Carolina has been to call on his supporters to vote as if he's on the ballot in November.

Yet those same Republican lawmakers who held tight with Trump through the primaries are now facing a general election environment and a very different electorate. They now have to contend not just with GOP voters, but Democrats who've always opposed the president, as well as disaffected independents who've drifted from Trump over economic concerns.

Retail gasoline prices are up. So is diesel. The cost of financing government debt has risen since the Iran war began, driving up the cost of mortgages, credit cards and consumer debt. And a confident White House that has unapologetically pursued all of its priorities at once, from tariffs to getting Trump's name on the Kennedy Center, is increasingly seen as unfocused on the costs Americans pay to go about their daily lives.

Trump's reservoir of support began to crack last week, when Florida Republican Maria Elvira Salazar cut a video telling Trump that his immigration crackdowns have gone "too far," as she battles to retain her House seat in a Miami-area district heavily impacted by the administration's deportation policies.

title: England players carrying World Cup scar - Saka
description: England winger Bukayo Saka says the team are still carrying the "scar" of their heartbreaking World Cup semi-final exit to Argentina.
fullText:
England winger Bukayo Saka says the team are still carrying the "scar" of their heartbreaking World Cup semi-final exit to Argentina.

Thomas Tuchel's team were on the verge of becoming the first England side to reach a men's World Cup final since 1966, but were stunned by two late Argentina goals as they fell to a 2-1 loss.

A thrilling 6-4 victory over France in the bronze medal match gave the Three Lions their best World Cup finish in six decades, but the wait for their second trophy goes on.

"Obviously, there is still a scar on us when you believed and everyone was so united and so confident we could do it," Saka said.

"Not just us, but the whole country we felt.

"You try to move on as soon as possible, but you know a scar is a scar, it decides to heal when it heals itself."

England get an immediate reminder of what might have been as they host world champions Spain at Wembley on Saturday (19:45 BST) in the first of four Nations League matches over the next two weeks.

"We are trying to draw a line under [the World Cup] now and focus on the new international season that we have coming up," Saka added.

"We have got four massive, difficult group games to try and qualify us for the Nations League [knockouts] that we are really focused on."

Meanwhile, Saka believes it is only a matter of time before his Arsenal team-mate Max Dowman, 16, earns a senior England call-up.

"I think so," Saka said. "His talent is insane. It's up to him how far he is going to go in football. His talent is crazy."

England Under-21 manager Lee Carsley concurred with Saka on Dowman's "amazing talent" but thinks the youngster staying with the under-19s during this international window is the best option.

"He is more than capable of playing in the under-21s," Carsley said.

"What I do think will happen with the age group he goes to is that he can play the minutes.

"He can also have that time to consolidate where he is in his career and play with his friends again and take that little bit of pressure off him.

"I have no doubt that Max is going to be with the under-21s.

"That is something I am keen to have a conversation with him and his parents, on the way we see his pathway going, because he is an amazing talent and someone we are very lucky to have."

title: What have we learned from the Championship so far?
description: As we enter the three-week international break, BBC Sport looks back at the opening block of Championship fixtures to see what we have learned so far.
fullText:
After a gruelling 37-day slog the Championship has begun a near three-week break for international football.

What have we learned from the opening eight-game block of the marathon 46-game campaign?

Just seven points separate the top 15 sides in the Championship after eight games - though Wolves and Pompey have yet to play their game in hand which was postponed due to Carabao Cup clashes.

It already feels like it could be a fascinating season with no stand-out team as yet, and the table backs it up.

Swansea lead the way, QPR, Stoke, Bristol City and Charlton are in the chasing pack, and West Brom have swapped the bottom five last season for the top five this.

Interestingly, since the Championship adopted its current name in 2004, only once has a team topped the table after eight matches and had fewer than the 17 points the Swans have currently earned - indicating this is a wide-open league this year.

Brighton were top of the pile in 2012 with just 16 points but the Seagulls ended up finishing fourth and went on to lose in the play-offs.

Six other sides have been in first place with 17 points before the Swans, but only two of those - Leeds in 2019-20 and Sheffield United in 2022-23 - won promotion.

Sorry to break it to Swans fans, however, but three of the other four did not even finish in the top 10.

There have been 277 goals scored already in the Championship this season.

That's 36 more than at the same stage last season, with one fewer match having taken place, and the second most ever at this stage since the Championship rebrand in 2004-05.

What do we put it down to? Well the stats suggest it is due to more direct play and quality on the flanks.

Only once in the past nine seasons have more goals come from crosses than the 47 so far this campaign.

Also, 44 of those 47 have come from headers, the most at this stage by some distance over the past five seasons, while nine have come from throw-ins - the second most at this stage in the past 14 seasons, behind only last season's 12.

That suggests a real shift in the way the game has evolved in recent times, given that from 2013-14 to 2020-21, by this point of the campaign, just 14 goals across those eight seasons - an average of fewer than two - came from throw-ins.

Bristol City's on-loan Crystal Palace full-back Rio Cardines has six assists already, the most by any player in Europe's top leagues.

Burnley began this season aiming to do something which had never been done before - become a six-time yo-yo club.

Six of Sean Dyche's eight full seasons in charge of Burnley were in the Premier League, winning promotion in his first and third full campaigns, but since his departure in April 2022 and their subsequent relegation, they have not stayed still.

Under Vincent Kompany, they won the 2022-23 Championship title with 101 points - before being relegated with just 24 points the next year.

With Scott Parker they went up again with 100 points, only conceding 16 goals, but were relegated with four games remaining last season leading to Parker's exit.

Nicky Hayen was the man entrusted with trying to get the club back to the top tier, but it has been a tortuous start to life at Turf Moor.

After a summer of wholesale changes in the squad, Hayen was appointed just 29 days before the Clarets' first game - 75 days later, eight games, four points and no wins has the Clarets bottom of the Championship.

Fellow slow starters Preston, Cardiff and Derby - the Rams having rescued a last-gasp draw at Turf Moor on Saturday - are the only other sides to be averaging fewer than a point per game.

The bad news for Burnley fans is that no side has ever been promoted from the Championship having been without a win in their opening eight fixtures and of the past 10 occasions only one - Brentford in 2018 - went on to finish in the top half.

The slightly better news is that seven of them avoided relegation, including Portsmouth two years ago and Sheffield Wednesday the season before that.

Fresh from a summer adventure with World Cup co-hosts Canada, Saints striker Cyle Larin is setting a frightening pace in the race for the Golden Boot.

The 31-year-old has started every game this season having made his move from Mallorca permanent after scoring eight goals in 16 appearances on loan during the latter half of last season.

Larin's seven goals in eight games have come at an average of one every 85 minutes and have helped Saints overhaul their four-point penalty following 'Spygate'.

Middlesbrough's big-money signing from Tottenham, Will Lankshear, is one behind, with the 21-year-old one goal ahead of Norwich's Mo Toure, whose five goals have come from just 11 shots this season for one goal every 91 minutes on the pitch.

Tottenham fans may already be wondering if Lankshear might be the one who got away and you can be sure Premier League clubs will be keeping a close eye on proceedings in the second tier this season, given forwards are likely to prove better value and less risky than signings from other European leagues.

Toure, sadly, will not get chance to add to his tally any time soon - the Australia striker will be out for several months due to a shoulder injury sustained against Bolton on Sunday.

West Ham were the pre-season favourites for promotion, just ahead of Wolves and, ahem, Burnley.

The Hammers took a while to get going on their return to the second tier for the first time in 14 years and took two points from their opening three games, including a shock home defeat by Charlton.

They found their feet with four straight wins, culminating in a 6-0 demolition of Wrexham, before rolling up their sleeves to escape with a 2-2 draw in the derby at Millwall on Saturday, which left them in second place after Swansea's win later that day.

The Hammers' 22 goals across their opening eight league games is the most in 93 years and six of the past seven sides to score that many in the opening eight games have gone on to win the title.

Given the talent on the field and the depth of the squad there's nothing in the opening eight games to suggest the Hammers won't last the pace and make an immediate return to the top flight.

The same can be said of Wolves, who are just three points off the top, with that game against Portsmouth in hand.

Wanderers left it late to salvage a draw at home to Blackburn in the season opener but have found their feet and shrugged off a 4-2 defeat at West Ham to take seven points from their next three games, including the trip to Birmingham and the Black Country derby at home to West Bromwich Albion.

Given they won only three of their 38 league games and earned just 20 points in total last season, four wins and 14 points from seven matches with an overhauled squad is a fine start for new man Cesar Peixoto.

Who'd have had QPR among their promotion contenders after they finished last season with just two points from their final six matches?

The Hoops have the second best defensive record in the Championship with just seven goals conceded in their opening eight games and their only defeat came at home to Middlesbrough, in a game the R's might well have claimed a point or more.

Converting chances has been their biggest issue.

They have 261 touches in the opposition box, second most in the division, and won 55 corners, again second most, but their shot conversion rate of 7.3% is 20th of the 24 teams in the division.

After losing their first three games, Stoke have taken 13 points from the next five to sit just four points off the top.

Mark Robins was under immense pressure after taking one point from the final six games of last season to end up 17th, having been in the promotion race before Christmas, but things appear to be looking up for the Potters.

They are one point behind West Brom, who have swapped the bottom four last season for the top five this, despite losing to Wolves last time out.

Lincoln have returned to the second tier for the first time in 65 years with a new management team, and a bang.

title: Scots recall Kerr & Thomas for World Cup play-offs
description: Sam Kerr and Martha Thomas are named in their first Scotland squad in almost a year for next month's World Cup round one play-offs against the Czech Republic.
fullText:
Sam Kerr and Martha Thomas have been named in their first Scotland squad in almost a year, as the experienced duo return for next month's Women's World Cup round one two-legged play-off against the Czech Republic.

Melissa Andreatta's side travel to Pardubice, east of Prague, on Friday, 9 October before welcoming the Czechs to St Mirren Park four days later, eyeing progression to another two-legged play-off against either Sweden or Lithuania with a place at next summer's tournament in Brazil at stake.

Liverpool midfielder Kerr - who has been playing out of position at right-back in the WSL - has yet to feature under Scotland women's Australian head coach, with the last of her 34 caps coming in February 2025 off the bench against the Netherlands, while Thomas - who joined WSL2 side Newcastle United in the summer - earned her 50th cap in October, in a friendly defeat by Switzerland.

Club-mate Freya Gregory - and Como defender Sophie Howard - who were forced to pull out of the last camp for the qualifying double-header against Israel, are also back in the squad.

Celtic midfielder, Maria McAneny - who last featured when scoring in a seven-goal thrashing of Luxembourg in March, returns too.

Defenders Leah Eddie and Kenzie Weir drop out, as do strikers Eilidh Adams and Laura Berry.

Mia McAulay was a late addition for the June double-header, but the Aston Villa youngster retains her place.

title: Hunting hidden gems - is there anywhere in the world left to scout?
description: Through live scouting and increasing data and footage, top clubs now have tabs on a large proportion of the world's talent.
fullText:
The world's biggest clubs were all aware of the teenage sensation turning heads for Universidad de Chile, the one dubbed his generation's Alexis Sanchez.

"When we signed Dario Osorio, it was not because no-one knew about him," Kristian Kjaer, technical director at Midtjylland, tells BBC Sport.

Osorio was on the radar of AC Milan, RB Leipzig, Salzburg and a number of other English and German clubs before he left Santiago for Denmark at the age of 19.

It was a carefully considered pathway. After three seasons in Scandinavia, the winger joined Crystal Palace on loan this summer with a £24m option to buy which would make him the most expensive sale in Danish Superliga history.

Midtjylland, where Brentford owner Matthew Benham was a majority stakeholder between 2014 and 2023, are renowned as one of the most innovative clubs in Europe for their use of analytics - from set-pieces to smart recruitment.

"We work on both pathways," explains Kjaer. "We have subjective scouting, more classic video scouting, live scouting, a network, people we trust in the club and also our partners. And then we have the data scouting.

"And Dario Osorio, we were aware of him long before we signed him."

From feet-on-the-ground to the increasing availability of footage, data analytics and artificial intelligence, Premier League clubs - whether buying direct from source or tracking players like Osorio's progress - have a large proportion of the world's emerging talent covered.

"That hidden gem kind of thing almost does not exist any 

"You would put this period as one of the most transformational in talent ID and recruitment," explains Sam Turner, head of operations at scouting and development platform Eyeball.

Clubs can now obtain an incredible level of detail on players across the globe before they have even made a senior appearance. Eyeball, for example, was founded five years ago to focus on those predominantly aged 13 to 21.

It is used by more than 60% of clubs in Europe's top five leagues, and a majority of Premier League sides, for access to more than 400,000 young players across 42 global markets from Europe to Africa and Latin America.

Winger Malick Yalcouye, a new 20-year-old star at Brighton, was tracked on the system since developing at Ivorian side ASEC Mimosas, likewise Bazoumana Toure, who is now at Newcastle.

The breadth of coverage is highlighted by other recent moves - Josue Caicedo left Ecuador's LDU Quito for Barcelona, Mustapha Nyassi swapped Gambia's Real de Banjul for Copenhagen and Nour Ashraf joined Leipzig from Egypt's ENPPI.

"The availability of data and footage has prompted a change in methodology," says Turner. "That has brought a load of benefits in terms of data-led recruitment, time saving, cost saving."

Eyeball takes north of 2,000 data points every match, typically from leading amateur clubs and elite academies who film and upload their fixtures.

The result is a huge database allowing analysts to watch all of a player's progressive passes, for example, discover who covered the most distance or simply ask 'find me a player like Ashley Cole'.

"There is always this human feel that can never be lost," adds Turner. "I like to think we have aided scouts and recruitment teams, supplemented them with the tools, data, information to be able to make more informed decisions on a more consistent basis."

Data, says Midtjylland's Kjaer, is "extremely important because it gives you an objective tool you can lean towards" when complemented by years of decision-making experience.

"We cannot just turn on the computer and it tell us who to sign and then we go sign them," he says. "We also need to know about the cultural background, the family background, to make sure they fit into our football club.

"Of course, data has given us opportunities. We sign young. So the sample size will simply be smaller for us because if we are waiting until it's big enough, Brighton and Liverpool and Brentford and other guys, they will sign the player in front of us."

"We can find interesting players all around the world," explains Kjaer.

"I like us to be open-minded. We are particular in the way we play and the way we sell. And therefore, we need to find these players who fit that style of play.

"When you have done your due diligence and you feel certain, pull the trigger. The pace in decision-making is also a hidden gem."

One country regularly mentioned is Uzbekistan, who played in their first World Cup this summer, while Turner says Azerbaijan is pioneering a national talent network and "very forward-thinking and motivated to progress the game domestically".

Then there is Japan, which Turner calls a "guiding star" in youth development for a system which takes players from grassroots, to school and college football and then the professional game. Think Kaoru Mitoma's thesis on dribbling techniques.

For European clubs, it makes identifying young Japanese prospects more complex.

Latin America, too, remains a hotbed of talent.

As former Midtjylland chairman Rasmus Ankersen, who has since worked for Brentford and Southampton, wrote in his book The Gold Mine Effect, a club such as Cruzeiro will reject 4,000 players under the age of 15 for every one they take in.

Brazilian clubs are naturally protective of their assets.

"They know eventually players will leave," says Turner. "But it is allowing them to leave at the right age where those clubs can benefit locally. And we are very invested in that."

Much of the region, however, remains "untapped" but recording games creates opportunities.

"It's just a visibility piece for a lot of these players that means they don't get picked up," says Turner.

"We have gone a long way in solving that for a lot of markets, but there are many more that can be picked up with brilliant players everywhere."

One of those markets continues to be Africa.

"There'll be thousands," says Thomas Randolph, founder of Delphlyx, when asked whether talented African players may have missed out on big moves in the past.

Delphlyx works with Premier League clubs and ownership groups, and others across Europe, the United States and Mexico, to provide information on the best - and most relevant - 14 to 21-year-olds in West Africa, often through data, live scouting and private tournaments.

"We have over 19,000 players in Africa on our platform that you could just sit right here in London and watch, then pick up the phone, call one of them and organise a trial or a transfer. That just wasn't happening before," adds Randolph.

With a projected average age of just over 18, Randolph says the region is a "young, growing, developing space" - a "sporting mecca". Football remains the main passion, though NFL and NBA are starting to invest in certain countries.

But Randolph disputes the idea African scouting is now saturated, citing a number of areas that remain relatively undiscovered, often because of conflict or logistics, with scouts drawn to the region's biggest cities.

"Zadok Yohanna is a good example," explains Randolph. "He moved to Brighton recently. He comes from Ikon Allah, which is a tiny and relatively unknown academy in northern Nigeria.

"The southern bit of Senegal is where Sadio Mane is from, where [Lamine] Camara is from, who Chelsea tried to sign, and there's only one team down there. So within all these big countries, there are certain regions that are less scouted."

Historically, it was agents who brought players out of Africa rather than scouts discovering them, whereas Delphlyx aims to help clubs identify and analyse certain talent first so scouts can visit specific tournaments or showcases to watch targets.

Randolph mentions eastern Mali, Togo, Guinea-Bissau and Burkina Faso but Benin, situated between Nigeria and Togo, is of particular interest for the way the country has invested federation grants in football infrastructure and pitches.

"One place they've used the Fifa money very well is Benin," says Randolph. "It's now produced probably a future female Ballon d'Or winner - Romaine Gandonou, who's 15, just played at the Under-20 World Cup, and got the likes of PSG, Barcelona, everyone after her.

"Benin is going to be a country that over the next few years will become very interesting."

Some Premier League clubs are buying directly from Africa. At 18, Senegalese defender Mor Talla Ndiaye has already been on the bench for Liverpool after arriving from Amitie, owned by ex-Newcastle and Chelsea striker Demba Ba.

Ndiaye was spotted at last year's Under-17 World Cup, where Burkina Faso midfielder Mohamed Zongo also impressed. He will join Chelsea and Strasbourg owners BlueCo's project when he turns 18 in two years' time.

"The Under-17 World Cup is a big one," says Randolph. "If your African nation plays there and you do well, you're going to get a good move."

Scouts have also been at the recent Under-17 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying and Delphlyx has helped organise trials for players from Senegal and Gambia at Premier League clubs.

The pool is narrowed, however, because players must obtain a Governing Body Endorsement to be granted a work permit or - most likely - take one of a club's four Elite Significant Contribution spots, which essentially comes down to how many youth or senior internationals they have played.

It's part of the reason young players initially move to European countries where regulations are less stringent and why Randolph believes Scottish clubs, where the same criteria does not apply, should be looking into the African market the way Scandinavians do.

Nordsjaelland are unique in that the Right to Dream academy - founded in Ghana in 1999 by former Manchester United scout Tom Vernon - bought the Danish club seven years ago to provide a pathway for its biggest prospects, which have included Mohammed Kudus, Simon Adingra and Kamaldeen Sulemana.

Brighton's Yalcouye and Newcastle's Toure made their first moves to Swedish clubs IFK Goteborg and Hammarby, while Midtjylland have a partner club in Nigeria, FC Ebedei. Coventry's Frank Onyeka played for both on his way to the Premier League, as did Paul Onuachu, now at Trabzonspor.

Like with Osorio, and others such as Guinea-Bissau forward Franculino, who left this summer for Trabzonspor, or Ivory Coast defender Ousmane Diomande, now at Nottingham Forest via Sporting, Midtjylland can highlight a track record of developing young players before selling them on.

"I see Midtjylland a bit like Silicon Valley for tech companies - we have produced so much talent over the years," explains Kjaer.

"We can focus only on the development. Of course, we need to win, but it's a bit more of a secure environment.

"What we say is, if you want to focus on your career as a football player, you have to come here because that is the only thing we do. That is what we are experts in."

There remains, however, undiscovered talent close to home. France, particularly Paris, boasts an incredibly rich talent pool.

A unique national youth league system, where amateur sides face professional academies - and regularly beat them - offers clubs the chance to witness unsigned prospects competing against the most gifted players in their age group.

"Scouts from all over the world come to Ile-de-France to look at players in our leagues," said Jamel Sandjak, president of the Ligue de Paris Ile-de-France, which boasts more than 1,000 clubs and 270,000 players.

"Most of the France national youth teams are full of our players. So our regional teams are playing at national level."

Last season, amateur side ES Nanterre, from the outskirts of Paris, won Championnat National Group B ahead of Champions League outfits Lens and Lille and second-tier clubs Reims, Bastia and Red Star.

Forward Exauce Luyindula was the division's top scorer for renowned amateurs AAS Sarcelles - where Riyad Mahrez played until he was 18 - and has since joined Ligue 2 Guingamp.

Other Eyeball, external partners enjoyed memorable victories, too. AFC Creil beat Lens at under-15 level, Olympique Rovenain's under-19s beat Nice and CS Bretigny's under-17s edged Paris St-Germain.

"Until recently, the vast majority of clubs were relying on the fact the best players are in the best academies or national talent systems, when actually a lot of those players were chosen by 12 or 13," explains Turner.

"A lot of the time that can be right, but also statistically the best players at 12 aren't always the best players at 18.

"There is such a high concentration of players in that region, there is not enough space. The best players aren't necessarily in the national systems."

fullText:
The French president sat down with David Muir for an exclusive interview.

In a wide-ranging exclusive interview with ABC News' David Muir, French President Emmanuel Macron said the "main objective" of his meeting with President Donald Trump on Monday was "to find the right deal in order to open" the Strait of Hormuz and address the escalating global energy crisis that has caused the price of gas, diesel and jet fuel to spike.

Macron told Muir that when the war started, "the Iranian regime discovered they had this card in their hands," in their ability to close the strait.  When asked whether that was a "blind spot" for Trump, Macron responded "I will not here blame anybody. We are where we are. I think the U.S -- I mean, your country -- is the one able to fix this issue, and we need you."

He added that the situation with the strait "was probably underestimated, and today we have to fix this issue."

When Muir asked the French president whether he would offer up his nation's military to help reopen the strait, Macron replied, "I don't want to engage in a confrontation with any country, but we are ready to be more engaged in order to protect some capacities in order to make this transit possible, yes."

Macron also criticized the decision to go to war in the first place, saying "Having a regime change by bombing a country is not something I think feasible." He added, "And for me, it's not a good option, because it doesn't work. And we did this mistake several times in the past decades."

Responding to Trump's complaints that "The U.S. is spending hundreds of billions of dollars, and [European allies] are not there for us," Macron told Muir France respects the U.S. and considers itself a "good ally."

Macron added "But when you want to engage people, you strategize with them, and you ask them before launching a war, and we decided not to join this war because we considered, and I still consider, it was not the right option."

With Macron warning about intensifying Russian threats towards Europe, Muir asked whether he believed Russian President Vladimir Putin when he said Russia has "no aggressive intentions."

"No," Macron responded. "I don't buy when President Putin say years ago he wanted peace and make peace. This is not true. And I don't buy when he say he doesn't -- he's not aggressive with -- with Europeans. This is not true."

Macron told Muir he had a "very good discussion" with Trump regarding Russia's war in Ukraine while in New York this week.

"My conviction is that your president has a fair assessment now of the situation, that Russia is not delivering what they wanted, that Ukraine is resisting with a lot of bravery and innovation, and that we have to help them," he said.

Asked about his relationship with Trump, Macron told Muir that he and Trump have a "very good" relationship, and while they sometimes disagree, "we have always been extremely frank to each other."

The French president said he believes Ukraine is an area where he has been able to "convince" Trump.

"I think on Ukraine we worked very hard, a few of us," he said. "I hope we change his mind. And the fact that he got the conviction that Russia was overrated."

During the interview Tuesday, Muir asked Macron about Trump's recent social media post showing a map with the U.S. flag sprawling across North America, including French territories off the coast of Canada.

"When asked about the map, you said, "People have strange ideas. They say strange things." Did you tell President Trump you thought it was strange?" Muir asked Macron.

"Yes, several times," Macron responded.

"Honestly, look at the situation today ... We have a war in Ukraine which is existential for the European security. We have war in the Middle East ... We have AI and all this technological race to, not to fix, but to coordinate and make sure that there is not a race to the worst between China and the U.S ... .We have sufficient topics to be fixed. Let's not create new conflicts and new tensions," Macron told Muir.

And as Trump calls AI fears a "hoax," Macron said he takes concerns that AI could pose a significant threat to humanity "very seriously."

"This is why we have to make it totally clear and to have visibility, cooperation, and build new regulation on these consequences," Macron told Muir, while calling for a global discussion on the rapidly developing technology.

"I think we should make a distinction between a pause for the frontier model and innovation and how precisely to be efficient regarding the misuses. ... It should not be just the decision of the U.S. government," he said. "It's a necessity to have a proper discussion between [the] U.S., China, Europe, and the rest of the world ... to deal with AI excesses and with AI risks for our economies and national securities."

Muir asked the French president about Trump's proposed "Triumphal Arch," which Trump has said is inspired by the Arc de Triomphe in Paris.

"President Trump wants to build an arch in Washington. He says it's gonna be like the one in Paris, but it'll blow it away," Muir asked Macron.

Macron responded he has seen pictures of the proposed arch, and had discussed the Arc de Triomphe with President Trump "several times."

Muir following up, asking "Is it gonna blow it away?"

"No," Macron responded. "Paris will remain Paris and the Arc de Triomphe remain the Arc de Triomphe...These monuments are bigger than ourselves."
