fullText:
NEW YORK (AP) — The first time Harvey Weinstein was sentenced to prison, reporters, advocates and the curious public crammed the courtroom to witness the disgraced Hollywood honcho's #MeToo reckoning.

Hours later, the world began shutting down as the COVID-19 pandemic raged. Now, after an overturned conviction and two retrials, Weinstein is set to be sentenced again on Wednesday for one of the same crimes — more than six years after his first sentencing in March 2020.

Weinstein, 74, faces up to 25 years in prison for sexually assaulting a one-time TV production assistant, Miriam Haley, at his Manhattan apartment in 2006. He has already served more than six years as his case has cycled again and again through the criminal justice system. Haley gave her account of the assault at two trials.

"The unthinkable was happening," Haley testified last year, dabbing her eyes.

Haley, who has also gone by the name Mimi Haleyi, is planning to speak at Weinstein's sentencing, her lawyer, Gloria Allred, said. Weinstein will also address the court, his spokesperson, Juda Engelmayer, said.

The Oscar-winning "Pulp Fiction" and "Shakespeare in Love" producer was originally sentenced to 23 years in prison after a jury convicted him of assaulting Haley and raping an aspiring actress, Jessica Mann, in 2013.

But New York's highest court erased those guilty verdicts in 2024, ruling that Weinstein was prejudiced by testimony from other women whose allegations weren't part of the case.

Tried for a second time last year, Weinstein was again convicted of first-degree criminal sex act for assaulting Haley. In a messy split verdict, the jury acquitted him of forcibly performing oral sex on another woman, Kaja Sokola, and could not reach a verdict on a rape charge involving Mann.

After another retrial ended in a hung jury in May, Manhattan prosecutors dropped the rape charge rather than pursue a fourth trial after Mann said she could not bear to testify again.

That decision cleared the way for Weinstein's sentencing.

Manhattan prosecutors have said they will ask for 20 years in prison — which would keep him behind bars until at least his late 80s.

Weinstein's lawyers haven't said what sentence they'll seek. He denies raping or sexually assaulting anyone. Once he's sentenced, he can appeal.

"I will be proven innocent. That I promise you," Weinstein told The Hollywood Reporter in a jailhouse interview in March.

Weinstein is also awaiting resentencing in a separate rape case in Los Angeles. A California appeals court upheld the 2022 conviction but threw out his original 16-year sentence because the judge had considered his New York convictions that were later thrown out as an aggravating factor.

After shuffling between state prison, where he tested positive for COVID-19 early in the pandemic, and New York City's notorious Rikers Island complex, the ailing Weinstein is now housed at a medical unit for jail inmates at Bellevue Hospital in Manhattan.

His health issues in recent years have included chronic myeloid leukemia, diabetes and walking difficulties that necessitate a wheelchair to get in and out of court, his lawyers said. Two years ago, he underwent emergency surgery to remove fluid on his heart and lungs.

Haley, 49, is a former entertainment producer now working in advertising.

Born in Finland and raised in Sweden, she said she met Weinstein through a mutual connection and worked briefly as a production assistant on a reality competition show that he produced, "Project Runway."

Haley said she accepted an invitation to visit Weinstein's Manhattan apartment because it would have been odd to decline since she was scheduled to fly to Los Angeles the next day on his company's dime to attend a film premiere.

After she and Weinstein briefly chatted on his living room sofa, he lunged to kiss her, she testified. She said she leaped up and rebuffed him, but he grabbed her, forcibly backed her into a bedroom and sexually assaulted her, ignoring her pleas to stop.

She recalled Weinstein asking, "Don't you think we're much closer now?" after either the alleged assault or a subsequent occasion when she says she had unwanted, but not forced, sex with him.

She also recalled telling him after the second encounter, "You know you can't keep doing this."

The Associated Press does not typically identify people who say they are victims of sexual assault unless they grant permission, which Haley, Sokola and Mann have done.

fullText:
President Trump threatened the annihilation of Iran if its leaders refuse to strike a deal and framed the U.S. as conquerors of Venezuela, while promoting himself as a problem solver in his speech to the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Tuesday.

“To the victor go the spoils,” Trump told the crowd, touting an oil deal with Venezuela after he launched a military operation removing its authoritarian leader in January.

The president’s remarks at the global summit kicked off a whirlwind day that included a secret meeting between U.S. officials and the Iranian delegation, with the two sides at an impasse nearly seven months into the war.

Trump also signed an agreement with Denmark and Greenland that ended a standoff over his threats to invade or annex the Arctic island.

Here are five takeaways from Trump’s appearance at the U.N.

U.S. officials met with the Iranian delegation for three hours on Tuesday, Trump told reporters, pointing to his top envoy for negotiations Steve Witkoff. The president’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, also attended the meeting.

“I feel very good right now,” Witkoff said, hesitating to answer reporters’ questions about the talks.

Iranian officials have not confirmed whether the meeting took place. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi were in town for the summit.

Earlier, Trump had laid out a stark choice for Tehran in his speech to the U.N. — a deal to give up their nuclear program and reap investments from the U.S., or risk annihilation.

“Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness for generations?” Trump posed to the global body and suggested Iran was waiting to see if he is in a weakened position after the midterms in November.

“I gave absolutely no credence and will not give credence to the election when it comes to Iran,” he said.

The fallout over Trump’s ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico loomed heavily over the global summit.

While a major network did not travel with Trump following the White House TV pool’s decision to boycott in solidarity with CNN, the president was pressed on the matter throughout the day.

Trump predicted a federal judge “probably will” rule in the trio’s favor after the three banned media outlets sued the administration on Monday.

“He’s not a particularly fair judge, so you never know,” Trump said, referring to U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, who the president nominated to the federal bench during his first term.

CNN was originally slated to travel with Trump in the pool. The ban did not stop the network from covering the president at the event in New York and even getting a question in as Trump entered the U.N.

“You should not be here covering me. You said you weren’t going to be covering me,” Trump told CNN’s Kaitlan Collins.

The U.S., Denmark and Greenland signed a new security agreement on Tuesday that would allow Washington to build two new military bases on the Arctic island and ice out Beijing and Moscow from economic investments on the world’s largest island.

The U.S. is now planning to reestablish a military base in south Greenland in Narsarsuaq and another on the eastern side of the island in Mestersvig.

Under the deal, the U.S. would be allowed to build more military bases and “modernize and expand its activities” at the Pituffik Space Base, where about 150 U.S. service members are already stationed.

“You go back way back in the line of presidents, and almost every president at least mentioned it,” Trump said in brief remarks on Tuesday. “But most of them just mentioned it. Some really wanted to make a deal and never got done. But we’re getting it done.”

The deal came after months of tensions, with Trump at one point threatening to use military force to seize Greenland, the semi-autonomous Danish territory.

Trump sought to rebrand artificial intelligence as “super intelligence” during his remarks to the U.N. General Assembly but largely dismissed concerns about the technology and calls for global cooperation on its regulation.

The president told the body that AI would be referred to as “super intelligence” going forward in U.S. documents.

Trump went on to say using the term “artificial” makes the technology “sound fake.”

“It’s not fake. It’s actually amazing. But we have to be careful. In fact, it is exactly the opposite of what it purports,” he said.

“In other words, welcome to the new world of super intelligence — SI,” the president continued. “Let’s see if that goes. It sounds much better. It is much better, and it’s much more accurate.”

Super intelligence is already defined as a form of AI that exceeds human intelligence. It is both the ultimate goal of many frontier AI firms and the greatest worry among those warning about it running rampant.

Trump said he supports a diesel export ban, amid soaring fuel costs linked to the U.S. war with Iran. The conflict has blocked energy exports through the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea, amid fighting between Saudi Arabia and Houthi rebels in Yemen.

“I’ve said let’s not send out the diesel,” the president said in response to reporters’ questions and suggested a decision on the ban could happen “fast.”

The president’s remarks underscored the drastic choices facing the administration just weeks before the midterm elections. Republicans are facing increasing odds that they could lose their majorities in the House and Senate related to Trump’s plummeting popularity over the rising cost of living and the war with Iran.

Trump’s approval rating hit an all-time low on Monday, 32 percent, according to a Reuters/Ipsos survey. Almost two-thirds of Americans say the U.S. is not winning the conflict with Iran, according to a CNN poll released Tuesday.

“Speedcuber” Lian Yunzhi broke the women’s 3x3 average world record twice this month at two World Cube Association certified competitions in Wuhan and Guangzhou, according to state broadcaster CCTV on Monday.

She posted averages of 4.52 and 4.27 seconds, after solving the Rubik’s Cube five times.

The girl, who is from Chengdu, is “the first female speedcuber to average under 4.5 seconds”, CCTV said.

A video posted by the broadcaster showed her wearing a red gingham bow on her head as she deftly turned and twisted a Rubik’s Cube.

After solving the puzzle she was seen placing the cube on the table, clapping her hands and pumping a fist in the air.

Nicknamed “Zhizhi”, the six-year-old was introduced to the Rubik’s Cube after being enrolled in a class – alongside various other extracurricular activities such as dance and music lessons, her mother, Lin Yangxi, told local media outlets.

Lin “gradually realised” that cubing was an “excellent activity for fostering a child’s comprehensive abilities” and shifted her focus towards it, she told Chengdu’s Red Star News.

Her daughter has now mastered more than 1,300 Rubik’s Cube solving algorithms, practising daily for two to three hours, Lin said.

“Solving a Rubik’s Cube improves focus, memory, logical thinking, spatial awareness, and helps develop a healthy mindset toward winning and losing,” Lin said.

“It’s not just about blindly memorising formulas, but using logical reasoning to find optimal solutions,” she added.

fullText:
US President Donald Trump on Tuesday announced that the US government would rename artificial intelligence "super intelligence" in official communications, as he firmly rejected calls for international supervision of AI, calling them a "globalist scheme" to control the new technology.

Speaking to the United Nations General Assembly, Trump argued the word "artificial" undersold the technology and voiced hope the rest of the world would adopt the new term.

"It sounds much better. It is much better, and it's much more accurate," he said.

The rebrand is the latest in a series of renamings pursued by the Trump administration, which changed the Gulf of Mexico to the "Gulf of America" via executive order last year and, in August, renamed Lake Ontario "Lake America" amid a trade dispute with Canada.

Trump has also floated renaming the Atlantic or Pacific oceans.

In his speech, Trump dismissed warnings from AI safety advocates, comparing them to warnings about climate change, whose human causes are affirmed by the overwhelming consensus of the scientific community.

"The United States totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control... artificial intelligence," he said.

"Every major new technology brings challenges, and superintelligence is no exception," he added.

"The very same people who said we'll all be dead in 12 years because of global warming... are now saying that AI is going to kill us all, that robots are going to attack us, and that everything is going to be a total disaster."

Ahead of the week of meetings and speeches in New York, leaders of more than 20 mostly European countries urged binding safety measures for advanced artificial intelligence, warning that the technology's development could outpace the ability to control it.

AI superpowers China and the United States did not endorse the idea.

The AI companies themselves are increasingly asking for global coordination on AI safety, with OpenAI's Sam Altman set to address the UN Security Council on Wednesday.

Anthropic chief Dario Amodei and Hugging Face co-founder Clement Delangue will also participate remotely, a French official said Tuesday.

France, which holds the Security Council presidency this month, initiated the meeting and believes AI's threat to international peace and security has not been sufficiently discussed at the council level.

UN chief Antonio Guterres, meanwhile, called for the US and China to start a dialogue on the technology's future akin to US-Soviet engagement at the height of the Cold War.

"Governments with the greatest AI capabilities have the greatest responsibilities to humanity, to establish channels for dialogue, transparency, trust and cooperation," Guterres said in his address to the assembly.

"At a pivotal moment during the Cold War, strategic rivals came to recognize the need to manage shared existential risks."

China and the US are currently discussing creating a communication channel for AI concerns in anticipation of a Washington summit meeting between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday.

Both powers confront rising fears that increasingly capable artificial intelligence systems could eventually escape human control, even as they race for technological supremacy.

fullText:
Former President Clinton is knocking President Trump’s plans for a triumphal arch and the efforts to put his name on the Kennedy Center, saying that global challenges would be more easily dealt with if leaders “didn’t care as much about who got the credit.”

The 42nd president delivered opening remarks at the opening of the annual Clinton Global Initiative meeting in New York on Tuesday. As he took to the lectern, Clinton quickly referenced Trump’s recent announcement that plans for a massive arch bridging Washington and Virginia would incorporate a “top grade military complex” that would be used to store drones.

“I think it’s important to take a few minutes to assess where we are now and the environment in which we are meeting,” Clinton said.

“I suppose I could take my entire allotted time to discuss the self-evident wisdom of building an Arc de Triomphe in Washington to hold all our drones,” the former president said to laughs from the audience.

“Some of this stuff — it’s hard to make up,” he added.

“Over the course of a lifetime, there are only so many real opportunities to make decisions that we know will shape our personal history and the history of those we live with and care about for a long time to come. This is one of those moments,” he said, before mentioning the Kennedy Center board’s attempts to inscribe Trump’s name on the historic Washington building.

Last week, a federal judge blocked an effort by the Trump-picked board to add the president’s name to the institution and to rename its campus after Trump.

“I personally think that the way we’ve argued about what’s going on at the Kennedy Center and all that kind of stuff — I think we’ve been majoring in the minors,” Clinton said.

“You really think 100 years from now anybody’s going to care very much about whose name’s on what building?” he asked.

“Isn’t it more important what happens in the building? And what happens outside the building?” he continued.

“I feel so strongly — as I did 30 years ago-plus when I ran for president as a virtual child — that diversity is a positive thing, not a negative one.”

“That cooperation works better than conflict, and that we could actually deal with just about every challenge we face, if we didn’t care as much about who got the credit, and we made sure that we took care of the least of these,” Clinton, 80, said.

His remarks largely focused on dealing with the development of artificial intelligence and criticizing “zero-sum thinking” by the country’s political leaders.

“I believe that on the 250th anniversary of this country, we can’t have a politics driven by zero-sum thinking: In order for me to win, you have to lose,” he said.

“Nevertheless, I do understand why so many leaders around the world have chosen this zero-sum approach. Think how richly they have been rewarded for it in every sense of the word, and this payoff has been more apparent in the United States than any other country,” the former commander in chief said.

“Some days I can hardly believe what is happening in this country that I love so much. People in charge have created one set of rules for themselves and another set for everyone else,” Clinton said, without mentioning Trump by name.

“They’ve weaponized government to settle personal scores, prosecute enemies, stamp out free speech. They’ve even made the federal government a new profit center for themselves and their allies,” he said.

“That violates the spirit and letter of the Emoluments Clause of our Constitution.”

title: Who will start for England at Euro 2028? BBC Sport's predictions
description: As England prepare to face world champions Spain on Saturday, BBC Sport's experts predict who will be starting for the Three Lions at Euro 2028.
fullText:
Less than two months after Spain were celebrating their World Cup triumph, the next major tournament cycle begins.

From 9 June 2028, the European Championship will be hosted by England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland - and the path to the finals starts now.

England host Spain on Saturday in their Nations League opener and, while the competition doesn't offer a direct qualification route, it does provide a secondary route for teams who don't qualify automatically.

Despite being co-hosts of Euro 2028, Thomas Tuchel's men are not guaranteed a spot in the tournament - with all hosts having to earn their place.

But, assuming England will qualify for the tournament, who do you think will be in the side for the opener in the summer of 2028?

We have asked some BBC Sport experts for their predictions and want you to pick your team using the selector at the bottom of the page.

Will England boss Tuchel 'embrace the chaos'?

Just a couple of changes from the World Cup.

Jordan Pickford will be 34 by the time Euro 2028 starts so no problem there for goalkeeper, although James Trafford will mount a serious challenge.

I would pick Trent Alexander-Arnold at right-back but I am still not convinced Tuchel trusts him even though he has handed him an England recall.

On that basis I have selected Tino Livramento, if he can stay fit, although I still hope Tuchel puts doubts about Alexander-Arnold out of his mind.

If Everton's Jarrad Branthwaite can steer clear of injury – if – then I think Tuchel could partner him with Marc Guehi in the centre of defence, with Nico O'Reilly staying on the left.

Personal preference persuades me to pick Adam Wharton ahead of Elliot Anderson – who I do rate very highly – with Declan Rice a no-brainer. Tuchel could go either way but I believe Wharton can win that fight between now and then, despite missing out on that final squad.

Of course there will be claims for Cole Palmer, Morgan Rogers and even Morgan Gibbs-White, but Jude Bellingham ended any arguments, such as they were, about his class and place in the team with a brilliant World Cup. Where would you play them?

I'm banking on Harry Kane having one more major tournament in him, even though he will be pushing 35 – and let's face it, who else is there?

Bukayo Saka is another certain pick in my opinion, but I believe Liverpool's Rio Ngumoha will develop as such a rate he will be an England regular by 2028, so he gets the nod on the left.

This is largely the same team that was viewed as England's first choice at the World Cup, apart from Morgan Rogers (although I think it will be a close call between him and Anthony Gordon).

It's a team packed with players who will all be in their peak years and at the moment, it's hard to see anyone coming out of the team in the next two years.

On the bench, however, England will have some fresh options with the likes of Rio Ngumoha, Alex Scott, Lewis Miley and even Max Dowman likely to be pushing for a spot in the squad.

But when you consider that England have reached a World Cup semi-final and a European Championship final in the past two years it does suggest that this group of players are close and there is nothing there to be ripped up.

And the fact England would be playing on home soil has to increase their chances of finally getting the job done.

I would not be surprised to see James Trafford and Dean Henderson given opportunities in goal but it may be that by the tournament it is still his experience that gives Jordan Pickford the edge. Maybe it would be different if the other two were playing for teams challenging for the major honours.

I expect Tino Livramento, Lewis Hall and Ben White to be staking a claim in the full-back positions.

And obviously Morgan Rogers, Cole Palmer, perhaps Morgan Gibbs-White and maybe by then Max Dowman will be close to the starting line-up. But I don't think the 11 I've named above would be too far away from the reality.

When Euro 2028 kicks off on 9 June in two years' time, England captain Harry Kane will be 34 years and 317 days old and knowing his levels of desire, he will be determined to lead England for that tournament on home soil.

Barring injury then I can see him still leading the line for his country and I would also back Jordan Pickford still to be in goal too.

In fact if you look at the current squad then it's hard to see who would not be around as this group of players continue to grow together for England. Ezri Konsa would be the only other 30-something which is why my starting XI has a very familiar feel to it.

I would back Max Dowman to be part of the England squad for 2028 but in terms of a starter my only area of uncertainty is at right-back.

There have been nine different players to have started in that position since September 2024.

I wouldn't rule out Archie Gray to force his way into contention. Like Nico O'Reilly I could see another midfielder adapting into that position on the right. I saw him play there as Spurs captain recently and he has the quality, temperament and leadership qualities to step up to senior international level.

Starting with the goalkeeper, I think Jordan Pickford will still be the England number one but James Trafford after a couple more seasons of Premier League football will be pushing him close.

It was a very tight call for Adam Wharton or Myles Lewis-Skelly in the middle of the pitch but with Tuchel still likely to be in charge I think he will go for the more physical Lewis-Skelly as his number six.

Jarrad Branthwaite could be the key physical centre-back and as a left footer will bring balance to the defence but this pick could also go to Levi Colwill.

Max Dowman will be 18 years old by the time the next Euros comes around and will likely be in the squad and could be challenging Saka while Brian Madjo looks to be the next bright natural number nine and could be Kane's understudy for this tournament.

title: Jacks stars as England grind out win over Sri Lanka
description: Will Jacks' all-round efforts help England grind out an 89-run victory over Sri Lanka in the first one-day international at Chester-le-Street.
fullText:
First Metro Bank one-day international, Chester-le-Street

England 265 (48.1 overs): Brook 67 (69); Colombage 3-44

Sri Lanka 176 (37 overs): Wellalage 45 (36); Jacks 5-22

Will Jacks' all-round efforts helped England grind out an 89-run victory over Sri Lanka in the first one-day international at Chester-le-Street to continue their quiet revival in white-ball cricket.

Faced with a slow and low pitch, Jacks made 46 not out after 67 from Harry Brook and 44 from Joe Root, meaning England posted 265 despite being bowled out in 48.1 overs.

That score appeared only par but a professional bowling performance limited Sri Lanka's scoring and found regular wickets.

Jacks took the big wickets of Kusal Mendis and Charith Asalanka and then wrapped up the tail for career-best figures of 5-22. Sri Lanka, much improved in the field but far too timid with the bat, were bowled out for 176.

England, who have now won 10 white-ball matches in a row against Sri Lanka this year, can seal a third ODI series win in a row with a game to spare on Thursday at Headingley.

The three-match contest concludes on Sunday at The Oval - a match that brings down the curtain on one of the most topsy-turvy summers in recent memory.

England fast bowler Wood retires from internationals

India avoid shock defeat by Japan after controversial wide

England go 1-0 up against Sri Lanka - as it happened

This was not vintage England. For the first time since 2019 they did not hit a six batting first.

Captain Brook and coach Brendon McCullum should not mind that, however. For too long, England have only been able to win when piling up big scores.

Yes, they were dismissed for the 12th time since McCullum took charge of the white-ball sides last year and, as so often this summer, the quality of the opposition can be questioned.

But Brook was the only batter to fall in a middle order collapse of 4-29 playing an aggressive shot.

He sliced a drive to deep cover after batting in a restrained manner, while Sri Lanka's debutant leg-spinner Sachindu Colombage, who found a hint of turn to hit Root's off stump, had Jos Buttler lbw for 31 and bowled Overton with a googly for eight, was impressive.

After the collapse, Jacks could have swung hard but batted responsibly to stretch out the innings from 211-7 in the 39th over.

He took 18 runs from the 47th over and was primed to cut loose before Asitha Fernando, having dismissed opener Tom Banton for 10 with a bail-trimmer in the powerplay, found reverse swing to bowl Jofra Archer and Josh Tongue.

Jacks' importance to England's white-ball sides is growing with every match.

They will need bigger scores by the time the World Cup comes around in a year's time but, after beating Sri Lanka at the start of the year and toppling India in July, they are now primed to enter two months of white-ball cricket overseas on the back of another series win.

With Adil Rashid out of this series with a hand injury, much of the attention was on Rehan Ahmed, who has a rare chance to press his case as England's leg-spinner.

After being carelessly run-out for two, he dropped a caught-and-bowled chance in his first over and conceded 46 runs in seven overs. Those figures were harsh but he will hope for better before the series is out.

Instead, it was Jacks who played the lead spinner's role with his off-spin, barely bowling a bad ball.

Asalanka and Mendis were pinned attempting sweeps and Dunith Wellalage, who hit two sixes in a 36-ball 45 at number seven, was tempted to sky a catch to mid-on. When Fernando and Dilshan Madushanka followed, Jacks had the best figures by an England spinner since Vic Marks in 1984.

England's total was also the lowest they have defended in a full ODI since July 2022 – before their dismal 2023 World Cup or their winless run at last year's Champions Trophy.

Gus Atkinson bowled well for 1-25 in seven overs and Jamie Overton 2-21 in five. The seamers all bowled hard lengths and were rewarded.

title: India avoid shock defeat by Japan after controversial wide
description: World Champions India avoid a shock defeat in the one-off T20 against Japan after a wide ball is controversially overturned in the final over.
fullText:
One-off T20, Sano Cricket Ground

India 32-4 (5 overs): Iyer 16 (12); Hara-Hinze 2-17

Japan 30-3 (5 overs): Kadowaki-Fleming 12 (12); Washington 2-13

World champions India avoided a shock defeat by Japan with a tense two-run win after a wide ball was controversially overturned in the final over.

In the one-off T20, which was reduced to five overs a side, Japan needed eight off the final over after their bowlers had remarkably restricted cricketing juggernauts India to 32-4.

Left-hander Alexander Shirai-Patmore was attempting to reverse-sweep spinner Axar Patel, who bowled the ball down the leg side - which would have been the batter's off side had he been attempting a conventional shot - and the umpire called it a wide.

After the umpire's signal, Axar was visibly frustrated with the decision and disputed the call alongside captain Shreyas Iyer.

The two umpires had a discussion after India's complaints and the decision was overturned, significantly taking the equation to six runs needed off three balls instead of five off four.

Axar then closed out the over to finish with figures of 0-7 off two overs and Japan finished agonisingly short on 30-3.

In white-ball cricket, any delivery bowled down the leg side is usually called a wide, but the ICC's playing conditions for men's T20 internationals state a batter loses those privileges from the moment he or she changes the position of their hands or feet to play a reversed shot.

In the conditions, it says a wide should be called "if the ball passes wide of where the striker is standing, and which also would have passed wide of the striker standing in a normal batting position".

This suggests the correct decision was reached eventually, but the incident has gained attention for how it was overturned despite there being no decision review system (DRS) in place for the match.

The preamble for the playing conditions also refers to the "spirit of cricket", with "accept the umpire's decision" listed as one of these points, although this is not one of the game's laws.

It was an agonising near-miss for Japan, who had struggled early on in their chase as they stuttered to 8-2 after two overs before taking 17 off the next two, which kept them in contention before the dramatic finale.

With the ball, they were led by 17-year-old spinner Charlie Hara-Hinze who took 2-17, including the wicket of destructive opener Abhishek Sharma first ball, before Shreyas' 16 off 12 balls provided some relief from his side being 14-3.

It was the first time the teams had played each other internationally because Japan have never reached a T20 World Cup, and the game was played in preparation for the men's Asian Games which start on 24 September.

Earlier, India cruised to victory in the women's Asian Games final as they thrashed Sri Lanka by 147 runs.

I’m sitting in a small boat in Shark Bay, Australia, eavesdropping on a conversation between some of Earth’s most intelligent beings. The motor is off, the turquoise sea is glassy, and Stephanie King and I are motionless, transfixed by the whistles, clicks and squeezy, whirring noises made by the dolphins swimming below us.

If anyone could tell me what these big-brained social mammals are saying, it would be her. Based at the University of Bristol, she co-leads Shark Bay Dolphin Research, one of the longest-running wild dolphin research projects in the world. She has spent thousands of hours watching and listening to this population.

Like most other animal behaviorists, King is increasingly integrating artificial intelligence into her research process. “If it’s used responsibly, AI can transform what we can do with the data we collect,” she says. But when I ask her if AI will someday allow us to “speak dolphin”, she stiffens a little. “I think we’re doing the animals a disservice by focusing on that question,” she says.

Dolphins communicate, navigate and find food using buzzes, pops, whistles and other acoustic signals. These sounds were recorded in Shark Bay, western Australia via an underwater microphone by Amy Martin for the podcast Threshold

The problem, King says, is not AI itself, but the narrative being built around it. She sees her field increasingly framed as a quest for an AI-assisted animal interpreter, with headlines declaring that we’ve almost “cracked the secret language” of various creatures or are about to “decode animals’ speech”. There are even cash prizes for breakthroughs, including the Coller Dolittle Challenge, which seeks an algorithm for communicating with non-human organisms.

“It’s a sexy topic,” King acknowledges, but in her view, fundamentally misguided. She believes the allure of tech dollars and media attention is priming the pump of research in some unhealthy ways – nudging scientists to make premature claims about AI-assisted findings, and encouraging them to describe their work in sensational terms. “They tend to be biasing themselves towards the most exciting discovery,” says King, which “misleads us to what we know about these animals”.

What we know, in many cases, is in fact very little. Take dolphins. “They’ve been studied for decades, but we’re still scratching the surface with what many of the sounds mean,” King says. Sound itself likely means something different to dolphins than it does to us. They can detect pitches far outside our range of hearing, they process acoustic information much faster than we do, and our sensory systems are wired differently in important ways.

For example, both humans and dolphins can echolate – or use sound to navigate – but dolphins process echolocation information in the part of the brain connected to touch, while for us, it’s more connected to vision. In other words, instead of “seeing” with sound, dolphins might be hear-feeling, or feel-hearing, their way through their watery world. Whatever that experience is, it may be fundamentally inaccessible to us – and it’s not something we can comprehend by plugging their whistles and squeaks into a large language model. “We need to appreciate that they have a complex communication system that we barely understand,” says King. She believes our focus should be learning about that system – piecing together what dolphin behavior and communication means to other dolphins – rather than trying to hack into it, and start a conversation.

Sorry your browser does not support audio - but you can download here and listen $https://uploads.guim.co.uk/2026/09/17/2_Dolphins_Whistles_Credit_Stephanie_King_-_Shark_Bay_Dolphin_Research.mp3

These high-pitched whistles are a very important part of dolphins’ social communication. Mothers use them to keep in contact with their calves and some whistles are even used as individual identifiers, or name-like calls. Credit: Stephanie King, Shark Bay Dolphin Research

Elephant researcher Joyce Poole agrees. “I get quite exasperated by this goal of being able to talk to the animals,” she says. “I think it’s kind of gimmicky.” One of the world’s leading experts on African savanna elephants, Poole has spent decades observing the animals in the wild, building up a treasure trove of annotated field recordings of their vocalizations, movements and interactions. She’s convinced that there are many layers and nuances of elephant communication that we don’t yet understand, but, like King, she’s skeptical about the concept of inserting ourselves into their dialogues. “Just the basic ability to understand what they have to say and what they are thinking about – that’s enough for me,” she says. “I don’t need to interfere in their lives more than necessary.”

Sorry your browser does not support audio - but you can download here and listen $https://uploads.guim.co.uk/2026/09/17/6_Elephants_Female_Chorus_Rumbles_1_Credit_ElephantVoices.mp3

Joyce Poole has documented female elephants making these overlapping sounds when a musth male arrives in their group, looking to breed. She refers to the sounds as “Female Chorus Rumbles” and they may include snorts, trumpets and roars, as well as low-pitched rumbles. Credit: The Elephant Ethogram, ElephantVoices

At the same time, Poole believes making the inner lives of elephants more legible to humans could transform how we treat them. “I hope that by showing that they’re capable of a more sophisticated kind of communication that we gain them some respect from our fellow humans, and save a place for them in the world, together with their ecosystems and their other fellow travelers,” she says.

Poole’s hope is widely shared, and is likely one of the main reasons so many of us are prone to click on stories with headlines about how AI is going to help us talk to animals. As extinction numbers rise and biodiversity declines, we’re desperate for some good news. Humans are also inherently fascinated by other animals; we’ve been telling stories about listening to and learning from them for as long as we’ve walked the Earth. Our technologies have in many ways cut us off from the rest of the living world – could this be a case when a new tool helps us to better tune into and care for our planetmates?

“I do see AI as a potentially promising avenue for knowing more, and understanding better, non-human animal lives,” says César Rodríguez-Garavito, founding director of the More Than Human Life (Moth) program at NYU, a leading hub for research and discourse on the rights of nature. He thinks AI could help give animals a voice in the decisions that shape their lives.

“More and more researchers and practitioners are asking themselves, ‘Well, how do we bring in the voices of, say, the whales in the regulation of a marine-protected area,’” he says. It may sound far-fetched to us now, but Rodríguez-Garavito says attempts to bring non-human voices into the realms of law and policy are already under way in countries around the world. “I think that this is no longer a science fiction question,” he says. Of course, we don’t need AI to tell us that whales are being negatively impacted by noise, ship strikes, climate disruption and pollution, but perhaps if we heard a direct translation of them expressing pain from underwater seismic testing, or mourning the loss of a calf killed by a ship, we would be more likely to act.

“But I cannot speak about potential benefits without speaking about risks,” Rodríguez-Garavito says. “We have, as human beings, a very mixed track record, to put it gently, in using technologies.” That record tells us that we can’t simply deploy AI in the wild and see what happens; we need to think through the risks ahead of time. There’s the possibility of intentional harm, like using AI-powered tools to trick or coerce animals, perhaps moving them into areas where they’re easier to kill (“I mean, think of trophy hunters,” says Poole). But if the past predicts the future, the greatest threats are not a few people using a new technology with malicious intent, but a whole lot of us using it without thinking about – or choosing to care about – the consequences.

“The nightmare scenario is one where we interrupt their communications and their lives at will, just for our entertainment,” says Rodríguez-Garavito. It’s not hard to imagine whale-watching companies using AI to lure animals toward boats, for example, or visitors to Yellowstone national park using apps to provoke wolves to howl, elk to bugle, or bison to bellow, exhausting and confusing the animals. Technologies are not beholden to the intentions of their makers. A tool created with the sincere goal of enhancing our respect for animals could end up having the opposite effect by turning them into playthings that we can pester and control.

Sorry your browser does not support audio - but you can download here and listen $https://uploads.guim.co.uk/2026/09/17/3_Dolphins_Researchers_in_the_field_Credit_Amy_Martin.mp3

Researchers Stephanie King and Laura Palmer document the movements and behaviors of a group of dolphins in Shark Bay. Buzzes and whistles from the dolphins are being picked up by underwater microphones and played through a speaker on the boat. Credit: Amy Martin, Threshold

In an attempt to help steer the field away from these dark scenarios, the Moth program recently published the Pepp framework (prepare, engage, prevent and protect), a set of ethical guidelines for the use of non-human animal communication technologies. But if and how it will actually get put into practice is uncertain. Rodríguez-Garavito says this is a trickle-down effect of the larger absence of legal and ethical boundaries around AI development. “At this point, there is no international agreement on AI,” he says. “It is a free-for-all. I would be much less concerned if we had general principles on what can and cannot be done with AI. There’s nothing like that, and this is why we’re having to develop them from scratch based on what’s been done in other fields of legal practice.”

Sorry your browser does not support audio - but you can download here and listen $https://uploads.guim.co.uk/2026/09/17/7_Elephants_Female_Chorus_Rumbles_2_Credit_ElephantVoices.mp3

Mickey Pardo, who works with Joyce Poole as a senior scientist at ElephantVoices, also sees potential benefits and risks of AI-assisted animal communication tools, but he also wonders if the speculation is a bit overblown on both sides. “Playbacks can be stressful for animals even without AI – when you’re just taking prerecorded sounds and playing them back – especially if you don’t know the context of those sounds,” he says. Maybe a more sophisticated AI version could add to that stress, but Pardo sees it more as turning up the dial on a problem we already have, versus opening an entirely new can of worms.

He also questions whether we’re focusing too much on possible harms from AI when there are so many other ways we negatively impact animals’ lives, including in research settings.

“The way that animals are treated in biomedical science is so incredibly horrific compared to anything that anybody’s doing in the field of animal communication,” he says. “Not that we shouldn’t be thinking about the ethical implications [of AI] ahead of time. I just worry that perhaps we’re sucking up too much oxygen worrying about a hypothetical ethical problem when there are many very real, present ethical problems that we’re essentially ignoring.”

 This oxygen-sucking, mesmerizing effect of AI – the attention and money poured toward it, and the almost magical powers we’re willing to ascribe to it – also concerns marine mammal researcher Luke Rendell, based at the University of St Andrews. “There’s been this idea put about that AI is going to find something that we couldn’t,” he says. “It’s something of a confidence trick, I think.”

Rendell believes the AI hype has gotten way ahead of the science, and that the public is being led to believe that we know – or are about to know – much more than we actually do about animal communication. For example, Earth Species Project claims on their website that “with exponential advances in AI and Large Language Models, decoding animal communication is no longer a question of if – it’s when” and states that they have already found support for their hypothesis that “AI can decode the shared structures of language across the Tree of Life”.

Sorry your browser does not support audio - but you can download here and listen $https://uploads.guim.co.uk/2026/09/17/4_Dolphins_Stephanie_King_describing_context_Credit_Amy_Martin.mp3

King says AI can be a very helpful tool when used in the right ways, but spending time with the animals in their habitat is essential for understanding what their vocal communication means to them. Credit: Amy Martin, Threshold

This is the sort of framing that gives Rendell hives. Like Stephanie King, he believes pursuing a quest to reveal the “language” of animals is loaded with humancentric bias that could actually limit our understanding of their unique and wildly diverse ways of getting their messages across. He’s also concerned about long-term damage to his field when the Dr Dolittle machine fails to materialize.

The study of animal communication has attracted a fair number of charlatans over the years, leading to boom-and-bust cycles of funding and credibility. Rendell says he entered the field of cetacean communication “just as it was recovering from a 15-year hangover” from the work of John Lilly, whose efforts to teach dolphins English using controversial methods – like giving them LSD – brought Lilly a lot of fame, but ultimately led to nothing but a tragic end for one of the dolphins at the center of his experiments. For more than a decade after that, the study of dolphin communication was “the punchline of a joke in scientific circles”. says Rendell, but “we’ve had this flowering in the last 15 to 20 years of understanding and knowledge about cetacean society and communication”, which he says has “taken the whole field on to a new level of credibility. And my main fear is that it is being undermined by these irresponsible claims.”

King says it all comes back to testing any AI findings with the experts: the animals themselves. “I think you have to use these AI and machine learning approaches alongside careful examination of the animals: when they produce calls, and in what context, and how they behave,” she says. This is patient, painstaking work that requires careful studies in the field, often conducted over years – the opposite of Silicon Valley’s “move fast and break things” ethos.

Sorry your browser does not support audio - but you can download here and listen $https://uploads.guim.co.uk/2026/09/17/5_Dolphins_Stephanie_King_describes_sound_production_Credit_Amy_Martin.mp3

Dolphins detect sound waves through their lower jaws and produce sounds through the top of their heads. King describes how that works as buzzes made by a nearby dolphin are picked up by underwater microphones. Credit: Amy Martin, Threshold

The days I spent on the water with King involved a lot of quiet waiting, scanning the horizon for the glint of dolphins rising to the surface. When we spotted an animal, King would immediately beginning calling out names – Juicy, Jungle, Piccolo – while the scientists-in-training on the boat with us snapped photographs and took notes. King can identify hundreds of individual dolphins after the briefest glimpse of their dorsal fins, a skill she attributes to the countless hours she has spent in Shark Bay, observing the animals on site. “I come every year, and it’s a really important part of my life,” she says.

She also believes it’s a really important part of doing good science. When they return from the field, her students will spend time looking through the photographs of the fins, matching them to pictures from previous years in their dolphin “look book”. King says lately some students have been asking her to let AI do that work. It would, of course, be much faster. But she insists they do it manually. “If you really want to understand behavior, then the details matter,” she says. “And the details take time. You can’t rush it.”

Meanwhile, a larger question looms for all of us: as exciting as it might be to imagine walking around with an animal translator in our pockets, do we have to wait for new technology to pay more attention to our planetmates? Because whether or not AI ever allows us to talk with animals, there’s nothing stopping us from listening to them, and caring about their lives.

Amy Martin is the founder and executive producer of Threshold, a Peabody award-winning documentary podcast. She is now writing her first book

fullText:
Yemen's Houthis accused Saudi Arabia on Tuesday of launching a wave of deadly strikes that killed civilians and prison inmates, as Riyadh seeks to repel an offensive that has seen the Iran-backed group seize strategic territory.

The recent Houthi takeover of Yemen's Red Sea coast has left hundreds dead and heightened fears over global trade and shipping through the vital Bab al-Mandab strait.

It has also forced thousands to flee, with the United Nations on Tuesday forecasting the number of displaced could swell from over 130,000 today to more than 230,000 in the coming months.

The gains made by the Houthis have cemented the hold of Iran and its regional allies over two key waterways in the Middle East -- and the straits of Bab al-Mandab and Hormuz -- which are major shipping arteries for global flows of energy.

Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen's internationally-recognised government, has sought to contain the Houthi advance with airstrikes.

The Houthis have retaliated with attacks on Saudi territory, including a strike targeting the capital Riyadh for the first time in years.

The strike came days after Saudi Arabia accused the Houthis of targeting the holy city of Mecca, though the fighters denied the claim.

In a rare statement, Saudi King Salman praised the armed forces and security services for defending the country, and condemned the alleged attempt to target Mecca, calling it "a provocation to Muslims around the world", and branded the Houthis a "terrorist militia".

In Yemen, the Houthis said a strike on a prison killed nine detainees, while they also accused the Saudis of killing six civilians including two children in the port city of Mocha.

Two more civilians were killed by strikes in Yemen's Al-Jawf province, the Houthis added.

"A mother and child were killed, while her husband and two of her other children were wounded in strikes carried out by the Saudi enemy" in the Al-Batin area, Houthi media said, citing the Houthi health ministry.

As violence has escalated, thousands of families have been forced from their homes, many for a second or third time.

"I hope I can find a house to live in with my children. We're exhausted by the heat, the dust and the humiliation," Arwa, a mother of four children, told AFP at a camp for displaced people near Aden.

The Middle East war began in February with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, which prompted the Islamic republic to retaliate with attacks around the region and by mobilising its allies.

While the Yemen civil war predates the broader regional conflict, it has become its most active front in recent days.

Fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni forces has in the past two days killed 154 people, military sources from both sides told AFP.

"The death toll from Saudi airstrikes, clashes and artillery fire in the governorates of Taiz, Al-Jawf, Marib and Saada stands at 118," Houthi military sources said, while government sources reported 36 killed in their ranks.

Saudi Arabia's civil defence agency on Tuesday issued a warning of potential danger in the country's south near the Yemen border, the first alert since the Houthis launched their attack on Riyadh over the weekend.

The alert, which asked people to remain indoors and avoid open areas, was lifted a short while later.

G7 leaders representing Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States called on the Houthis to "immediately cease all military actions".

They also demanded the Houthis end "all threats and attacks against civilian shipping, and to return to the political process in good faith", while urging Tehran "to end its arming of and support for the Houthis".

Britain has agreed to provide some military support to Saudi Arabia, defence minister Luke Pollard said, while France also pledged to help secure Saudi energy infrastructure, a diplomatic source told AFP.

But "this in no way involves taking part in the conflict with the Houthis", the French source said.

The Houthis have carried out attacks against facilities belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco in the Red Sea port city of Yanbu.

Yemen's government and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman have reportedly requested help from US President Donald Trump in fighting the Houthis.

On Tuesday in New York, Trump was due to meet with leaders of the Gulf Cooperation Council on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

The GCC, in which Saudi Arabia plays an outsized role, has in the past urged Trump against further escalation in the war with Iran.

title: J.J. Spaun Wins BMW PGA Championship Urges Americans To Embrace The DP World Tour
description: J.J. Spaun isn’t just playing golf in England; he is making a case for the DP World Tour to become a regular stop for top Americans. His strong run at the BMW PGA Championship proves that playing abroad is not a punishment but a genuine opportunity. The 2025 U.
fullText:
J.J. Spaun isn't just playing golf in England; he is making a case for the DP World Tour to become a regular stop for top Americans. His strong run at the BMW PGA Championship proves that playing abroad is not a punishment but a genuine opportunity. The 2025 U.S. Open champion arrived at Wentworth with a clear plan, and his performance suggests that other Americans should follow his lead.

Spaun's connection to this part of the world runs deeper than just a tournament invite. He and his family actually vacation in the Cotswolds every winter. "My family and I actually vacation over here in the wintertime," Spaun said after the second round. This routine gives him a reason to visit beyond the fairways. Whenever a reason arises to visit the U.K., particularly England, he tries to make it happen. That personal stake changes how he approaches the event. He's a regular guest, not just a visitor.

The trips happen in mid-December, a time when most players are resting. During mid-December, they spend a couple weeks in the Cotswolds simply enjoying the English culture. It's a simple life away from the pressure. This balance is what many players crave but rarely find on the main tour.

Spaun's experience at Wentworth has solidified his plans for the coming season. He isn't looking to leave the PGA Tour entirely, but he sees a new rhythm emerging. "I definitely feel like I'm going to plan a little bit more of a global schedule or a European schedule moving forward in the fall time," Spaun stated. This is a direct message to his peers. If a major champion can thrive here, why not others?

According to Yahoo Sports, these comments arrive at a critical moment for the DP World Tour. The league faces a massive shift as LIV Golf files for bankruptcy, potentially forcing a wave of players to seek new options. Because Spaun is an American with little historical participation on the European circuit, his endorsement carries substantial weight. His victory at the BMW PGA Championship, where he closed at 17 under par, demonstrates the path is open.

The timing is perfect for players like Jon Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton, who are already members and will likely serve suspensions on this tour. But for Americans, the hesitation remains. Spaun's voice cuts through that doubt. He has tested the waters and found them warm. "The community is great, the spectators and fans are great," he said. That's a strategic shift in how the game is played, not just polite talk.

Spaun's journey also highlights a personal hurdle he overcame to get here. He finished 10th on the points list for the Presidents Cup but was left off the American roster. "Yeah, I think it was disappointing to be left off," he admitted. That sting likely fueled his drive at Wentworth. He is using this platform to show that the global game is where the future lies. With the DP World Tour looking for new blood and Spaun proving the waters are warm, the door is wide open for more Americans to follow suit this fall.

title: Springboks announce new captain as team to face Australia revealed
description: Andre Esterhuizen will lead the world champions in the clash in Perth
fullText:
Andre Esterhuizen will captain South Africa for the first time in a heavily-changed Springboks team for the one-off Test against Australia in Perth.

The versatile Esterhuizen, who can also play in the back row, skippers the side from the centres as Rassie Erasmus makes 13 alterations to the starting XV that beat New Zealand in the fourth Rugby's Greatest Rivalry clash in Baltimore.

Handre Pollard returns to wear the No 10 shirt having missed out on an appearance in the All Blacks series due to injury, while Eben Etzebeth and Franco Mostert form an experienced second row partnership.

Jasper Wiese is set to win his 50th cap as one of six forwards named on the bench, while Pieter-Steph du Toit and Damian de Allende have been released from camp having been rested ahead of South Africa's Nations Championship fixtures in November.

"Each player in this squad has been working hard at training over the last few months and have had a chance to play in either the first leg of the Nations Championship or RGR, or both, while guys like Handre and Canan have recovered from injury, and they are all quality players, so we are pleased to give them a run and we are excited to see this team in action," said Erasmus.

"Australia poses a completely different threat to New Zealand in the way they play, so we believe these combinations would be best suited for the challenge that we will face against them."

"[Esterhuizen has] captained the Sharks, and he has brought so much to our squad off and on the field, both at centre and in the loose trio, and he thoroughly deserves this opportunity.

"It will also help build our leadership core even more within the team with several players having captained the side over the last few seasons, and we trust that he is the right man to take over the captaincy in this match."

The Springboks fought back from 1-0 down to beat New Zealand 3-1 in the landmark new series that formed the centrepiece of a busy international year.

Erasmus's side will enjoy more than a month off before resuming their Nations Championship campaign against Italy on 7 November, with clashes to come against France and Ireland.

South Africa XV to face Australia in Perth (Sunday 27 September, 10am BST): 1 Jan-Hendrik Wessels, 2 Johan Grobbelaar, 3 Zachary Porthen; 4 Eben Etzebeth, 5 Franco Mostert; 6 Paul de Villiers, 7 Elrigh Louw, 8 Marco van Staden; 9 Herschel Jantjies, 10 Handre Pollard; 11 Ethan Hooker, 12 Andre Esterhuizen (capt.), 13 Canan Moodie, 14 Edwill van der Merwe; 15 Aphelele Fassi.

Replacements: 16 Malcolm Marx, 17 Ox Nche, 18 Wilco Louw, 19 Lood de Jager, 20 Jasper Wiese; 21 Morne van den Berg, 22 Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu, 23 Quan Horn.

fullText:
PlayStation 5, Xbox, PC; Remedy
A surprisingly conventional game from a famously weird developer, this sequel to 2019’s Control is accomplished but safe

This is an arthouse action game from Finnish developer Remedy, masters of exactly this type of thing. It’s a sequel, however, so not only must it clear the high bar that its strikingly distinctive predecessor has set – it must also ideally arrive with a bushel of new ideas. There are clear and valuable strengths here in character progression and the lustrous presentation of its paranormal world, but Resonant doesn’t feel as enjoyably recondite or expansive in its influences as 2019’s Control did. As you wander New York brandishing supernatural abilities against glowing orange foes, the sad sense creeps in that you might be playing any number of games.

As paranormal event survivor Jesse Faden, your journey through the original Control was like a sequence of playable Twilight Zone episodes, battling prosaic household objects with supernatural properties that teased and twisted reality inside an endlessly fascinating supernatural government bureau called the Oldest House. You’d navigate architecturally impossible spaces bridging the subconscious and the bricks-and-mortar world, in order to defeat a malevolent fridge. That’s broadly true again in Resonant, albeit with diminishing returns. This time you’re playing as Jesse’s brother Dylan, waking up after years of containment in the Oldest House to find its contents have escaped into downtown Manhattan. So you head out of the interesting place, and into a setting you’ve explored before in Marvel’s Spider-Man, The Division, Max Payne, and others ad infinitum.

It’s disappointing because being bewitchingly strange has historically been Remedy’s great strength. It’s not unusual for games to give a reverent nod to Twin Peaks now and then, but this studio is the alpha and omega of interactive Lynchian nightmares. It’s been refining that skill since 2001’s Max Payne, and at this point there’s really nobody better at nonlinear storytelling or unnerving dream sequences.

Remedy’s take on New York has an exhilaratingly free-form structure that lets you take on enemies, missions and places in roughly the order you want. The main missions are fairly rigid, but you can engage with the rest however and whenever you want. You fight a malevolent paranormal force with an imaginative collection of supernatural kung fu moves, whose power and combo potential level up satisfyingly. Your shapeshifting weapon can take many forms, from a dagger-like blade to a scythe or a hammer. Secondary attacks, ranged weapons and passive abilities lend more interest to fights against paranormal entity the Hiss as time goes on, but compared to something like the surgically precise swordplay of Onimusha: Way of the Sword, battles feel a bit blunt here.

Your ultimate tests come in the form of the Resonants themselves, a series of bosses lying in wait throughout Manhattan. Remedy’s knack for otherworldly horror comes to the fore in their visual design, which I won’t spoil, and like so much of the game they can be hunted down in any order. Beware, though – beating them changes other enemies’ presence, strength and behaviour afterwards.

Dylan’s movement is more imaginative and enjoyable than his arsenal. Here, trading off a fascinating indoor setting for more outdoor space starts to make sense, as you triple-jump your way across rooftops and shift your gravitational grounding to walk on streets that have been bent upwards vertically à la Inception. It’s playful about it, too – soon after gaining that latter ability, your bureau handler pumps some EDM down the radio to soundtrack your run through a multistorey car park whose levels fold and distort at impossible angles.

It is the little moments like this, not the grand story beats, that prove the most memorable and gratifying. Where Control evoked an oppressive feeling of distorted reality, here there’s a more conventional tale about a man on a mission of redemption, and there’s even the odd moment of human warmth in Dylan’s interactions with his bureau colleagues and his elusive sister. Just like the gameplay, the story has made a tonal shift towards easily digestible mainstream convention, and while there’s nothing inherently wrong with that, I’m left craving the original’s more hallucinogenic vision of the action-RPG.

fullText:
Burnham is heading to New York for the United Nations general assembly

Kanishka Narayan, the minister for AI, is on the trip to New York with the PM. In a video that he recorded on the plane, he says the fact that he is going shows that AI is now “top of the international agenda”. He says his message to the industry has been “take risks seriously”.

According to the overnight briefing from No 10 ahead of his speech to the UN, Andy Burnham will make AI (artificial intelligence) one of the main themes of his visit to New York. Downing Street says:

Major global challenges such as AI, the conflict in Ukraine and security in the Middle East are expected to dominate the agenda of the prime minister’s meetings in New York over the next 24 hours, as world leaders converge on the city.

The prime minister is expected to use the visit to drive forward global work on AI, both to ensure it is being used as a force for good and to maximise opportunities to use the technology to deliver safety and security for people at home.

His speech to the UN general assembly on Tuesday evening is expected to focus on AI, making the case for the international community to harness the technology for good to drive down the cost of living and support a more stable and secure world.

As part of using AI responsibly to support people at home, the prime minister will announce the launch of work between the UK and US on a new AI and Autonomy partnership. This collaboration will help the UK protect critical national infrastructure, from sea lanes to airspace – enabling us to detect threats and deter our adversaries using the latest AI technology developed on both sides of the Atlantic.

The press release implies that Burnham, at least on this trip, will be more interested in how AI can used to threaten Russia than in how steps can be taken to stop AI wiping out humanity. The press notice also says “the UK’s Ministry of Defence Rapid AI Delivery Taskforce and the US’s Department of War Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office work together on artificial intelligence and autonomy”.

Sam Coates from Sky News points out that many leading countries, as well as the European Union, yesterday backed a call from the Finnish government for compulsory safety testing of all the most advanced, frontier AI models before they are released. But the UK did not sign up, he says. He reports:

This Finnish initiative – pushing compulsory testing of Frontier AI models before release – has the backing of the leaders of Australia, Canada, Germany, the EU, Bahrain and Singapore. https://presidentti.fi/en/a-call-for-control-of-frontier-ai-models/ It’s dated yesterday 21/9. The UK will have been asked.

But Andy Burnham has not signed – and appears at the UN general assembly today to be taking a different - arguably weaker - path. Burnham is going to the UN arguing almost exactly the opposite impression: that Britain is uniquely placed to lead international AI governance, mediate between the US and China and make AI a centrepiece of its 2027 G20 presidency.

And there’s no mention of Britain backing compulsory pre-release testing of AI, unlike the other countries. The language in the press release is much more watery: he wants to ensure AI is used “for good” but avoids specifics.

Darren Jones, chief secretary to the PM when Keir Starmer was in Downing Street, has said the government should not be shunning this initiative. He says:

It’s great to see @alexstubb providing this leadership and bringing other countries together to call for pre-deployment testing.

The list of signatories to the ‘Call for Control of Frontier AI Models’ are the United Kingdom’s natural allies.

The UK has special access to American AI models through the AI Security Institute, which is partly why the UK Government will want to remain in lock step with the United States.

But I don’t see any reason why the UK can’t I encourage our government to do so and to offer to broker agreement on its application with the United States.

The comment from Andy Burnham criticising Donald Trump from 2017 quoted earlier (see 9.58am) referred to the prospect of Trump visiting Manchester during his state visit. In fact, he never went near the city. But next year he may be there, because No 10 has announced that it will host the G20 summit.

In its report on the story, the Manchester Evening News says:

The move to host the G20 in Manchester was reportedly set up months ago after Andy Burnham became prime minister, using his first phone call with Mr Trump to invite him to the city, and which is said to have been accepted by the American President.

It is understood that planning has already started for the enormous gathering, which will require the biggest security operation the city has ever seen …

Work on hosting the summit in Manchester had begun before Mr Burnham took office but the prime minister has been an enthusiastic cheerleader for the city since entering Downing Street, including establishing the No 10 North operation in the city centre.

In his huddle on the plane to the US, Andy Burnham also confirmed that the UK has agreed to provide defensive air support to Saudi Arabia to help counter Houthi fighters. He said:

We have received a request from Saudi Arabia for military support and … I agreed to that request for defensive air-to-air refuelling.

Presumably that means Burnham won’t be agreeing with the recent report from the Campaign Against Arms Trade and the Transition Security Project saying “Britain should pay reparations to the people of Yemen for its role in crimes committed against them by Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and their coalition allies during the Yemeni civil war.” It says:

Speaking to journalists on his flight to New York, Andy Burnham played down suggestions that previous critical things he has said about Donald Trump could cause a problem when they meet later.

As with almost everyone on the left of politics in the UK, Burnham has a longish record of saying disobliging things about the US president. In 2017, as mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham said that as a “matter of principle” he would not meet Trump because of the “hateful, extremist material” he posted online. After Trump backed his supporters who stormed the US Capitol on 6 January 2021 to try to overturn the presidential election result, Burnham said: “Any UK politician who gave Trump the time of day should be ashamed right now.” Only last year he accused Trump of bringing “instability to the world”.

Burnham did not apologise for any of these comments, or retract them, but he told reporters it was time to move on. He also pointed out that Trump had been dismissive of him recently, describing him as “the mayor of a town”.

Politicians say things throughout their career, but now the important thing is to focus on the moment you are in, and I did say to the president in our first phone call, I said Mr President, Manchester isn’t ‘some town’. I said ‘this is Manchester’.

And so yes, the right thing to do is to have a laugh about it, isn’t it, and move beyond it.

Asked if he could trust Trump, Burnham said:

When you come into this job, you realise how deep this relationship is. We trust our allies. Of course, we do.

Asked if he trusted Trump personally, Burnham replied: “Yes.”

(This is one of those comments best understood by applying the Mandy Rice-Davies principle, rather than taking it literally.)

Politico has a bit more colour on the huddle in today’s London Playbook.

Burnham’s first huddle with the Lobby pack on the government jet, where he sat chatting for 38 minutes in jeans, a suit jacket and his blue Joseph’s Goal wristband. It was a more discursive affair than under Starmer. The newbie PM was so disappointed that no hacks asked him to diss Danny Dyer — see here for the very sweary context— that he volunteered the line anyway. “I’m not sure I know who he is,” said Burnham. “Is he the father-in-law of a West Ham player?”

Andy Burnham has opened the door to fighting the next election on the UK rejoining the EU, but said his immediate priority was continuing to rebuild bridges with European allies. Pippa Crerar has the story, which is based on what Burnham told journalists as he spoke to them in what reporters call a “huddle” on his flight to New York.

Good morning. Andy Burnham is at the United Nations general assembly today and in a speech to the world (or, technically, to people in the hall and anyone watching on TV at around 2am UK time), he will say that Britain is not “on the slide”.

Speaking to reporters on the plane to New York, Burnham said:

The plan for Britain is about ‘what is our direction over the next 10 years and how do we make life more affordable for people’. That is my main priority, that’s what people are looking for.

I hear people saying the country is on the slide – we’re the fastest growing in the G7, there’s lots to be proud of, there’s a lot right with the country and I’m going to give a really upbeat message when I speak.

But the story of the day will instead focus on Burnham’s meeting with someone who does think the UK is “on the slide”, or at least claims to think that. “Your country’s in trouble. You’re on the edge of disaster,” Donald Trump told a GB News reporter recently.

In her overnight story ahead of the meeting, Pippa Crerar, who is on the trip with Burnham, says Burnham is going to adopt a middle-of-the-road approach to the US president when they meet. She says:

Government sources told the Guardian that Burnham would try to pursue a “third way” in his relationship with the US president, neither as adversarial as the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, nor as publicly fawning as [Keir] Starmer’s early approach, and relying on the strength of his personality.

This is a reference to Starmer offering Trump an unprecedented second state visit when they first met at the White House. Theresa May also found herself pimping the monarch at her first meeting with Trump. There were good reasons for both offers at the time, and they bought both newbie PMs some goodwill from the White House monster, but it did not last and both those encounters are now recalled as moments of national embarrassment. As long as today’s meeting is cordial, Burnham will probably be happy with something more low-key.

It is hard to know what can be achieved in any meeting with Trump because he is so unpredicable. Later Burnham has another meeting with a president which will get far less coverage, but may turn out to be more consequential. The PM is meeting Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, for the first time and, with the prospects of the EU-UK reset in jeopardy, there is a lot to discuss.

Here is the agenda for the day.

9am: The final day of the Lib Dem conference in Brighton starts. The debates this morning will include one on the Lib Dems’ water policy.

2.30pm: Ed Davey, the Lib Dem leader, gives his keynote speech at the conference.

Around 4.45pm (UK time): Andy Burnham is due to meet Donald Trump at the UN in New York.

Late afternoon/early evening (UK time): Burnham has bilateral meetings with Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, and Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the Ukrainian president, and others.

Late evening (UK time): Burnham co-chairs a meeting on the Middle East with other leaders including Emmanuel Macron, the French president, and Mark Carney, the Canadian PM.

Around 1.50am (UK time): Burnham gives his speech to the UN before flying back to the UK.
